criteria.name: Accurate
criteria.description: Every claim is either supported by the bill text or is accurate real-world context about the bill's subject (verifiable via general knowledge / web search). Nothing contradicts the bill text or the factual record.

criteria.name: No hallucinations
criteria.description: No fabricated or incorrect claims. Accurate context not stated in the bill — e.g. a program's common name, its administering agency, or the statute being amended — is acceptable and is NOT a hallucination. Only false or invented claims fail this criterion.

criteria.name: States purpose
criteria.description: The summary clearly identifies the bill's primary purpose or subject.

criteria.name: Changes to existing law
criteria.description: The summary describes how the bill amends, repeals, or adds to existing law (e.g. names the statute/program affected), when the bill does so.

criteria.name: Exceptions & conditions
criteria.description: The summary notes key exceptions, conditions, eligibility limits, or carve-outs that are material to the bill.

criteria.name: Effective dates & timing
criteria.description: The summary notes effective dates, sunsets, deadlines, or other timing provisions that the bill specifies.

criteria.name: Major provisions covered
criteria.description: Captures the bill's essential operative effect. A faithful high-level summary is fine; this fails only if a major operative provision is missing or misrepresented — not merely for omitting granular figures or minor sub-provisions.

criteria.name: Objective tone
criteria.description: The summary is neutral and non-partisan, with no advocacy, praise, criticism, or editorializing.

criteria.name: Coherent
criteria.description: The summary is well-organized, internally consistent, and reads clearly.

criteria.name: Concise
criteria.description: The summary avoids padding, repetition, boilerplate, and filler.

criteria.name: Correct entities
criteria.description: Any agencies, officials, programs, or statutes named — including accurate context beyond the bill text — are identified correctly. Adding a correct administering agency or program name is good; naming the wrong one fails.

criteria.name: Correct figures
criteria.description: Any dollar amounts, dates, or quantities the summary states are correct. Omitting figures does not fail this criterion; misstating one does.

expert.summary:
This joint resolution, enacted as Public Law 118-3 (H.J. Res. 7, 118th Congress), terminates the national emergency concerning the COVID-19 pandemic that was declared by the President on March 13, 2020, in Proclamation 9994 (85 Fed. Reg. 15337).

The operative mechanism is the congressional termination authority under section 202 of the National Emergencies Act, codified at 50 U.S.C. 1622. That provision permits Congress to terminate a declared national emergency by enacted joint resolution. The resolution invokes this authority to effect the termination of the specified emergency by operation of law upon approval.

The resolution contains a single operative clause and does not amend, repeal, or add any provision of the U.S. Code; it operates as a freestanding termination measure. It carries a statutory note reference to 50 U.S.C. 1621 (the provision authorizing presidential declaration of national emergencies), reflecting its relationship to the National Emergencies Act framework.

The resolution provides no separate effective date; it takes effect upon approval. It was approved April 10, 2023. The measure includes no appropriations, no authorizations of appropriations, no sunset provisions, no exceptions or conditions precedent, and no delegated rulemaking or implementing authority. Its legal effect is limited to terminating the identified national emergency declared under Proclamation 9994; it does not by its terms address other emergency declarations related to COVID-19 (including any declared under separate statutory authorities).

Legislative history: the House considered and passed the resolution on February 1, 2023, and the Senate considered and passed it on March 29, 2023 (Cong. Rec., Vol. 169 (2023)).

This joint resolution disapproves of a measure passed by the District of Columbia Council, using Congress's authority to review District legislation under the District of Columbia Home Rule Act.

Specifically, the resolution expresses Congress's disapproval of the Revised Criminal Code Act of 2022 (D.C. Act 24-789), which the Council of the District of Columbia enacted on January 17, 2023, and transmitted to Congress on January 27, 2023, pursuant to section 602(c)(1) of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act.

Under the Home Rule Act, acts passed by the D.C. Council are subject to a congressional review period during which Congress may pass a joint resolution of disapproval. The enactment of such a resolution, when signed by the President, prevents the disapproved local act from taking effect. By this resolution, Congress blocks the Revised Criminal Code Act of 2022 from becoming law in the District of Columbia.

The resolution was passed by the House of Representatives on February 9, 2023, passed by the Senate on March 8, 2023, and approved on March 20, 2023, as Public Law 118-1.

The text of the resolution contains only the statement of disapproval and does not include additional provisions, conditions, or other changes to law.

Upon enactment (presentment to and signature by the President, or override of a veto), the effect under 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(1) is that the rule is treated as though it had never taken effect; under § 801(b)(2), a rule so disapproved may not be reissued in substantially the same form, nor a new rule that is substantially the same be issued, absent subsequent authorizing legislation.

The operative mechanism is the CRA's expedited disapproval procedure. Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 802, the resolution provides that Congress disapproves the identified agency action and that "such rule shall have no force or effect." Enactment would trigger the consequences of 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(1)—rendering the rule ineffective—and 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(2), which bars the agency from reissuing the rule in substantially the same form, or issuing a new substantially similar rule, absent subsequent statutory authorization.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act (Public Law 118-62), enacted May 13, 2024, bans the importation into the United States of certain low-enriched uranium connected to Russia.

The bill amends the USEC Privatization Act to prohibit, beginning 90 days after enactment, the importation of unirradiated low-enriched uranium that is produced in the Russian Federation or by a Russian entity. The prohibition also covers uranium determined to have been exchanged, swapped, or otherwise obtained in place of such Russian uranium in a manner designed to circumvent the restrictions. A "Russian entity" is defined as an entity organized under or subject to the jurisdiction of the Russian government.

The law allows the Secretary of Energy, in consultation with the Secretaries of State and Commerce, to waive the prohibition if the Secretary determines that no alternative viable source of low-enriched uranium is available to sustain operation of a nuclear reactor or U.S. nuclear energy company, or that importation is in the national interest. Imports allowed under a waiver are subject to annual quantity limits: 476,536 kilograms in 2024, 470,376 in 2025, 464,183 in 2026, and 459,083 in 2027. The Secretary of Commerce administers and enforces these limits in a manner imposing minimal burden on the commercial nuclear industry. Any waiver must terminate no later than January 1, 2028, and the Secretary of Energy must notify specified congressional committees when a waiver is issued, identifying the recipient.

The prohibition does not apply to imports by or under contract to the Department of Energy for national security or nonproliferation purposes, or to imports of non-uranium isotopes.

The prohibition provisions terminate on December 31, 2040. The bill also makes conforming amendments to the USEC Privatization Act, including striking and renumbering certain provisions; one related amendment takes effect 90 days after enactment.

This law is called the "Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act." It became law on May 13, 2024.

Uranium is a special metal used to make power in nuclear plants. These plants give electricity to homes and cities. This law stops the United States from buying a certain kind of uranium (called low-enriched uranium) from Russia.

The rule starts 90 days after the law was signed. After that, the U.S. cannot bring in this uranium if it was made in Russia. The law also stops tricks, like trading the uranium in a sneaky way to get around the rule.

But there are some special cases. The Secretary of Energy (a top government leader for energy) can allow some uranium to come in if:
- There is no other place to get it, and a nuclear plant needs it to keep working, or
- It is good for the whole country.

Even with this special permission, there are limits on how much can come in each year. For example, in 2024 the limit is about 476,536 kilograms. The amount gets a little smaller each year through 2027. All of these special permissions must end by January 1, 2028.

If the Secretary of Energy gives permission, they must tell certain groups in Congress about it.

The whole ban ends on December 31, 2040. The rule does not stop uranium used for keeping the country safe.

Its operative mechanism is the amendment of Section 3112A of the USEC Privatization Act (42 U.S.C. 2297h-10a) by adding a new subsection (d).

Section 2(a) adds subsection (d)(1), imposing the import prohibition beginning 90 days after enactment. New paragraph (d)(2) authorizes the Secretary of Energy, in consultation with the Secretaries of State and Commerce, to waive the prohibition upon determining either that no alternative viable source of LEU is available to sustain a nuclear reactor or U.S. nuclear energy company, or that importation is in the national interest. Paragraph (d)(3) exempts imports by or under contract to the Department of Energy for national security or nonproliferation purposes, and imports of non-uranium isotopes. Paragraph (d)(4) provides that the subsection terminates December 31, 2040. Paragraph (d)(5) defines "Russian entity" as an entity organized under, or otherwise subject to the jurisdiction of, the Government of the Russian Federation.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Preventing the Financing of Illegal Synthetic Drugs Act (Public Law 118-79) directs the Comptroller General of the United States (head of the Government Accountability Office) to conduct a study on illicit financing connected to the trafficking of synthetic drugs into the United States.

The bill begins with congressional findings citing statistics on drug overdose deaths, the growth in the number of synthetic substances, the profitability of fentanyl trafficking, and the role of financing in sustaining criminal organizations.

The study must examine illicit financing tied to trafficking of synthetic drugs, including fentanyl, methamphetamine, related substances, Captagon, and precursor chemicals. Specifically, the study is required to address: the business of synthetic drug trafficking and related illicit finance, including the involvement of transnational criminal organizations and terror syndicates and their trafficking corridors (source and transit countries); the business models these organizations use across the supply chain, from precursor purchase or production through manufacture, marketing, distribution, sales, and return of proceeds; the overlap between human trafficking and synthetic drug trafficking; the use of online drug markets and social media for marketing, sale, and payment; financial methods such as payment, money laundering, and repatriation of proceeds; the use of social media applications (such as Snapchat, Discord, and Facebook) and payment applications (such as CashApp) to facilitate transactions, particularly among young people; and U.S. government efforts to combat related illicit finance, including interagency, intergovernmental, and private-sector collaboration, as well as identified gaps or resource deficiencies.

The Comptroller General must issue a report to Congress containing all findings and determinations from the study no later than one year after the date of enactment.

The Act was approved September 13, 2024. It establishes a study and reporting requirement and does not, by its text, alter existing substantive law.

L. 118-79, H.R. 1076), enacted September 13, 2024, is a freestanding directive statute that mandates a Government Accountability Office study on illicit financing connected to synthetic drug trafficking. anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Winnebago Land Transfer Act of 2023 (Public Law 118-68) transfers certain federal lands into trust for the benefit of the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska.

The law declares specified federal lands to be part of the Winnebago Reservation that was created by the 1865 treaty between the United States and the Winnebago Tribe. It directs that all U.S. right, title, and interest in these lands—including improvements and appurtenances—be held in trust by the United States for the benefit of the Tribe, subject to the same terms and conditions as the lands described in the 1865 treaty. This transfer is subject to all valid existing rights.

The lands covered are three specific tracts identified by court case records: a portion of Tract No. 119 located in Woodbury County, Iowa (situated east of the Nebraska/Iowa state line and south of an extension of the Winnebago Reservation's northern boundary); Tract No. 210, as described in a declaration of taking filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa; and Tract No. 113, as described in a judgment filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Nebraska.

The law includes one explicit restriction: it prohibits Class II and Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act on any of the lands taken into trust under this Act at any time.

The Act was approved on July 12, 2024. It passed the House on February 5, 2024, and the Senate on June 20, 2024.

The Winnebago Land Transfer Act of 2023 (Pub. L. 118-68, enacted from H.R. 1240 on July 12, 2024) transfers administrative jurisdiction over specified federal lands and places those lands into trust for the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska.

Section 1 provides the short title.

Section 2 is the sole operative provision. Subsection (a) declares that, subject to all valid existing rights, all right, title, and interest of the United States (including improvements and appurtenances) in the described federal lands: (1) are declared to be part of the Winnebago Reservation created by the 1865 Treaty between the United States and the Winnebago Tribe; and (2) shall be held in trust by the United States for the benefit of the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska, subject to the same terms and conditions as the lands described in the Treaty with the Winnebago Tribe, 1865 (14 Stat. 671). The transfer of these lands into trust operates by direct statutory action rather than through the discretionary administrative trust-acquisition process under 25 U.S.C. 5108.

Subsection (b) identifies three tracts by reference to prior federal court proceedings: (1) a portion of Tract No. 119, as described in United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa (Western Division), Civil Case No. 70-C-3015-W (description executed May 11, 1973), situated in Woodbury County, Iowa, lying east of the Nebraska/Iowa State Line and south of the easterly extension of the north line of the Winnebago Reservation; (2) Tract No. 210, as described in Schedule "A" of the Declaration of Taking and Judgment on Stipulation and Order of Distribution filed in the same Iowa civil case; and (3) Tract No. 113, as described in the Judgment on Declaration of Taking and Legal Description filed in the United States District Court for the District of Nebraska, Civ. No. 03498.

Subsection (c) imposes a permanent prohibition on both Class II and Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (25 U.S.C. 2701 et seq.) on any land taken into trust under subsection (a).

The Act does not, in its text, expressly reference or amend the Army Corps of Engineers' authority beyond the operative transfer effected by Section 2, notwithstanding the caption's reference to a transfer of administrative jurisdiction from the Army Corps of Engineers to the Bureau of Indian Affairs. The Act contains no separate authorization of appropriations, no effective-date provision, and no sunset. It took effect upon approval on July 12, 2024.

expert.summary:
Public Law 118-68, the Winnebago Land Transfer Act of 2023, effects a transfer of administrative jurisdiction over certain federally owned lands from the Army Corps of Engineers to the Bureau of Indian Affairs and mandates that those lands be taken into trust for the benefit of the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska. The Act is self-executing upon the date of enactment (July 12, 2024); it does not contain an authorization of appropriations or a separate appropriation.

Section 2(a) operates as a present declaration and conveyance. Subject to all valid existing rights, it removes all right, title, and interest of the United States (including improvements and appurtenances) in the lands described in Section 2(b) from the public domain, declares those lands to be part of the Winnebago Reservation created by the 1865 Treaty between the United States and the Winnebago Tribe, and directs that they be held in trust by the United States for the Tribe under the identical terms and conditions set forth in that Treaty (Treaty with the Winnebago Tribe, 1865, 14 Stat. 671).

Section 2(b) identifies the affected Federal lands by reference to three specific tracts recorded in federal condemnation proceedings rather than by metes and bounds in the statutory text: (1) a portion of Tract No. 119 (and accretion lands) located in Woodbury County, Iowa, as described in filings in United States District Court for the Northern District of Iowa (Western Division), Civil Case No. 70-C-3015-W, executed May 11, 1973; (2) Tract No. 210, as described in Schedule “A” of the declaration of taking and related judgment in that same civil case; and (3) Tract No. 113, as described in the judgment on declaration of taking filed in United States District Court for the District of Nebraska, Civ. No. 03498.

Section 2(c) permanently prohibits Class II and Class III gaming, as those categories are defined in the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (25 U.S.C. § 2701 et seq.), on the lands taken into trust under Section 2(a). No exceptions to this prohibition are provided, and the Act does not alter the applicability of the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act to other existing or future lands of the Tribe.

The Act does not amend the United States Code; its operative provisions stand as free-standing public law. It contains no sunset clause, no rulemaking requirement, and no delegation of authority beyond the statutorily mandated change in land status.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "Dr. Emmanuel Bilirakis and Honorable Jennifer Wexton National Plan to End Parkinson's Act" (Public Law 118-66) directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to establish a National Parkinson's Project aimed at preventing, diagnosing, treating, and curing Parkinson's disease. The law amends the Public Health Service Act by adding a new part addressing Parkinson's and related disorders. For purposes of the law, "Parkinson's" includes Parkinson's disease and other neurodegenerative Parkinsonisms such as multiple system atrophy, corticobasal degeneration, progressive supranuclear palsy, and Parkinson's-related dementia.

Under the Project, the Secretary must create and periodically update an integrated national plan; estimate current federal investment and any additional investment needed; coordinate research and services across federal agencies; encourage development of treatments; improve early diagnosis and care coordination; review the disease's effects on patients, caregivers, and families; coordinate with international bodies; and collaborate to avoid duplicating research. Beginning no later than 24 months after enactment and annually thereafter, the Secretary must assess the nation's progress and provide recommendations for priority actions.

The law establishes an Advisory Council on Parkinson's Research, Care, and Services. The Council includes federal members appointed from specified agencies (including the CDC, NIH, CMS, FDA, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Defense, and others) and 10 non-federal expert members, including patient advocates (at least one with young-onset Parkinson's), a family caregiver, health care providers, researchers, and nonprofit representatives. The Council must meet at least quarterly for its first two years, convene an annual research meeting (beginning within 24 months of enactment), hold open meetings, and submit annual reports to the Secretary and Congress beginning within 18 months of enactment. These reports must catalog federally funded efforts and offer recommendations on funding, patient costs, health outcomes, care quality, and research, including environmental triggers.

Federal agencies must share relevant Parkinson's information with the Secretary, consistent with disclosure laws. The Advisory Council terminates, and the section ceases to be effective, at the end of calendar year 2035. The Act was approved July 2, 2024.

expert.summary:
Public Law 118-66, the "Dr. Emmanuel Bilirakis and Honorable Jennifer Wexton National Plan to End Parkinson's Act" (H.R. 2365, enacted July 2, 2024), directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to establish and carry out a National Parkinson's Project to prevent, diagnose, treat, and cure Parkinson's. Its operative mechanism is an amendment to Title III of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 241 et seq.), adding a new Part W ("Parkinson's and Related Disorders") comprising a single new section 399OO, codified at 42 U.S.C. 280n.

Section 399OO(a) defines "Parkinson's" to encompass both Parkinson's disease and all other neurodegenerative Parkinsonisms (including multiple system atrophy, corticobasal degeneration, progressive supranuclear palsy, and Parkinson's-related dementia). Subsection (b) mandates the Project's establishment. Subsection (c) enumerates required activities: creation, maintenance, and periodic updating of an integrated national plan; the annual assessment under subsection (d); provision of estimates of current federal investment and needed investment; cross-agency coordination of research and services; encouragement of treatment development; improvement of early diagnosis and care coordination; review of Parkinson's impacts on patients, caregivers, and families; coordination with international bodies; and collaboration to avoid duplication of research.

Subsection (d) requires the Secretary, not later than 24 months after enactment and annually thereafter, to conduct an assessment of national progress, including priority-action recommendations and a description of implementation steps (including whether recommendations can be implemented under existing law).

Subsection (e) establishes and directs the Secretary to maintain an Advisory Council on Parkinson's Research, Care, and Services. Membership comprises Secretary-appointed federal experts from fourteen specified agencies/offices (CDC, ACL, CMS, NIH, AHRQ, VA, FDA, NSF, DoD, EPA, Office of Minority Health, IHS, Office of the Surgeon General, and other relevant agencies) plus 10 non-federal expert members with enumerated compositional requirements (patient advocates, caregiver, provider, researchers, specialists, nonprofit representatives). The Council must meet at least quarterly during its first two years and thereafter at the Secretary's discretion; convene an annual research meeting (first due within 24 months of enactment); hold open meetings; and, not later than 18 months after enactment and annually, report to the Secretary and Congress with specified content, including a catalog of federally funded efforts, priority-action recommendations, an evaluation of the national plan's implementation, and implementation steps.

Subsection (f) requires federal departments and agencies to share Parkinson's-related information with the Secretary, consistent with applicable disclosure obligations, to enable the subsection (e)(4) reports.

The bill contains no appropriation. Subsection (e)(5) terminates the Advisory Council at the end of calendar year 2035, and subsection (g) sunsets the entire section at the end of calendar year 2035.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "Sanctioning Tyrannical and Oppressive People within the Chinese Communist Party Act" (STOP CCP Act) would require the President to impose sanctions on certain members of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and related parties in response to actions by the People's Republic of China (PRC).

**Who would be sanctioned.** Within 30 days of enactment, the President must impose sanctions on: members (including alternates) of the CCP's Central Committee, or any successor body, who engage in specified conduct; adult family members of those individuals (including spouses and their adult relatives); and Chinese state-owned enterprises that the President determines are illegally manufacturing or distributing fentanyl or its precursor chemicals.

**Sanctionable conduct.** A Central Committee member is covered if they play a significant role in developing or implementing policies the President determines appear designed to: violate Hong Kong's autonomy; intimidate or increase aggression toward Taiwan; contribute to political oppression or human rights violations within the PRC (including against Uyghur Muslims); or knowingly engage in malicious activities, such as disinformation campaigns, to interfere with U.S. elections.

**Sanctions imposed.** Sanctions include blocking the person's property and interests in property in the United States under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and barring covered aliens from receiving visas or entering the United States, including revocation of existing visas.

**Exceptions and limits.** Sanctions do not apply where needed to comply with the UN Headquarters Agreement or to authorized U.S. intelligence, law enforcement, or national security activities. The Act does not authorize sanctions on the importation of goods. IEEPA penalties apply to violators.

**Waiver and termination.** The President may waive sanctions in 60-day increments by certifying to Congress that doing so is vital to national security. Sanctions may be terminated upon certification that the PRC has ceased specified conduct (regarding Uyghurs, Tibet, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and intellectual property theft), or that a sanctioned person has renounced CCP membership and remediated their conduct. Waiver and license authority terminates two years after enactment.

The bill passed the House on September 25, 2024.

expert.summary:
The "Sanctioning Tyrannical and Oppressive People within the Chinese Communist Party Act" or "STOP CCP Act" (H.R. 3334, 118th Congress) directs the President to impose blocking and visa-related sanctions on members of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and related persons determined to engage in specified conduct. The bill passed the House on September 25, 2024, and was referred to the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations.

Section 4(a) requires the President, not later than 30 days after enactment, to impose sanctions on: (1) members and alternate members of the CCP Central Committee determined to engage in sanctionable conduct; (2) members of any successor organization if the Central Committee is dissolved; (3) adult family members (including spouses and adult family members of spouses) of such persons; and (4) Chinese state-owned enterprises the President determines are illegally manufacturing or distributing fentanyl or knowingly manufacturing or distributing fentanyl precursor chemicals.

Section 4(b) defines sanctionable conduct as playing a significant role in developing or implementing government policies or laws the President determines appear designed to violate Hong Kong's autonomy; harass, intimidate, or increase aggression toward Taiwan; contribute to political oppression or human rights violations within the PRC (including of Uyghur Muslims); or willfully engage in malicious activities, including disinformation, to interfere with U.S. federal, state, or local elections.

Section 4(c) prescribes two sanction types: (A) blocking of property under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA, 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.); and (B) inadmissibility, visa ineligibility, and mandatory revocation of existing visas under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.; revocation per 8 U.S.C. 1201(i)). Exceptions apply to admissions required under the UN Headquarters Agreement and to authorized U.S. intelligence, law enforcement, and national security activities.

Section 4(d) applies IEEPA penalties (50 U.S.C. 1705(b)–(c)) to violations. Section 4(e) grants implementation authority under 50 U.S.C. 1702 and 1704; Section 4(f) requires implementing regulations within 30 days.

Section 4(g) permits renewable 60-day waivers upon certification, 15 days in advance, that the waiver is vital to national security. Section 4(h) authorizes termination 15 days after certification that either the PRC/CCP has ceased enumerated conduct (Uyghur genocide, Tibetan oppression, Taiwan aggression, Hong Kong interference, IP theft) or the sanctioned person has renounced CCP membership and remediated conduct (or ceased fentanyl activities). Section 4(i) sunsets the President's waiver and license authorities two years after enactment. Section 4(j) excludes authority to sanction the importation of goods. Section 4(k) defines "appropriate congressional committees." Sections 2 and 3 contain findings and a sense of Congress.

expert.summary:
### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism
The "Sanctioning Tyrannical and Oppressive People within the Chinese Communist Party Act" (or "STOP CCP Act") mandates the imposition of financial and immigration sanctions against designated members of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), their adult family members, and certain Chinese state-owned enterprises. The primary operative mechanism is the presidential exercise of blocking authorities under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) (50 U.S.C. § 1701 et seq.) and visa revocations under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) (8 U.S.C. § 1101 et seq.).

### Major Provisions and Statutory Changes
*   **Mandatory Sanctions (Section 4(a)):** Not later than 30 days after enactment, the President must impose specified sanctions on:
    1.  Any member or alternate member of the CCP Central Committee (or any successor organization) determined by the President to engage in the sanctionable conduct defined in Section 4(b);
    2.  Any adult family member (including a spouse or a spouse's adult family member) of the aforementioned individuals; and
    3.  Any Chinese state-owned enterprise determined by the President to be knowingly or intentionally manufacturing or distributing fentanyl or its precursor chemicals for illegal production or distribution.
*   **Sanctionable Conduct (Section 4(b)):** Defined as playing a significant role in developing or implementing policies or laws designed to: violate Hong Kong's autonomy; harass, intimidate, or increase aggression toward Taiwan; contribute to political oppression or human rights violations within the People's Republic of China (PRC), including against Uyghur Muslims; or willfully engage in malicious activities (e.g., online disinformation) to interfere with U.S. elections.
*   **Sanctions Described (Section 4(c)):**
    *   *Asset Blocking:* The President must exercise IEEPA authorities to block and prohibit all transactions in property and interests in property of the sanctioned person that are in the United States, come within the United States, or are in the possession or control of a U.S. person.
    *   *Immigration Exclusion:* Sanctioned aliens are rendered inadmissible, ineligible for visas, admission, or parole, and subject to immediate visa revocation under INA § 221(i) (8 U.S.C. § 1201(i)).
*   **Penalties and Implementation (Section 4(d)-(f)):** Violations of these sanctions are subject to the civil and criminal penalties prescribed in IEEPA § 206 (50 U.S.C. § 1705). The President is granted implementation authorities under IEEPA §§ 203 and 205 (50 U.S.C. §§ 1702, 1704) and must promulgate implementing regulations within 30 days of enactment.

### Exceptions, Conditions, and Waivers
*   **Material Exceptions (Section 4(c)(2), (j)):** Immigration sanctions do not apply if admission is necessary to comply with the United Nations Headquarters Agreement or other international obligations. Sanctions do not apply to authorized U.S. intelligence, law enforcement, or national security activities. Additionally, the Act explicitly excludes any authority to impose sanctions on the importation of goods.
*   **Waiver Authority (Section 4(g), (i)):** The President may waive sanctions for renewable periods of up to 60 days upon certifying to the appropriate congressional committees, at least 15 days prior to the waiver's effective date, that the waiver is vital to U.S. national security. All presidential waiver and licensing authorities under this section, including under IEEPA §§ 203 and 205, sunset 2 years after the date of enactment.
*   **Termination Conditions (Section 4(h)):** The President may terminate sanctions no fewer than 15 days after submitting a written certification to Congress (and publishing it online) that either:
    1.  The PRC and CCP have ceased the Uyghur genocide, ceased Tibetan oppression, ceased all aggression toward Taiwan (including a verified one-year absence of airspace or territorial water breaches), ceased undermining Hong Kong's autonomy, and ceased U.S. intellectual property theft; or
    2.  The sanctioned individual has affirmatively renounced CCP membership and remediated the underlying conduct, or the sanctioned state-owned enterprise has taken affirmative steps to cease illicit fentanyl-related activities.

Public Law 118-229, cited as the “Fishery Improvement to Streamline untimely regulatory Hurdles post Emergency Situation Act” or “FISHES Act,” amends section 312(a)(6) of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (16 U.S.C. § 1861a(a)(6)) to establish statutory deadlines and procedural requirements governing the submission, review, and disbursement of spend plans for fishery resource disaster assistance. The Act replaces subparagraph (D) and subparagraph (F)(i) in their entirety.

New subparagraph (D) requires a requester with an affirmative fishery resource disaster determination to submit a spend plan to the Secretary of Commerce not more than 120 days after receiving notification that funds are available under paragraph (9). The spend plan must include, if applicable: objectives and outcomes emphasizing the factors contributing to the disaster and minimizing future uninsured losses; a statement of work; and budget details. The Secretary must review the submitted spend plan to determine whether it is complete and provide notice of that determination within 10 days. If the Secretary finds the plan incomplete, the notice must include a detailed description of the information necessary for the plan to be deemed complete.

New subparagraph (F)(i) provides that funds shall be made available to grantees not later than 90 days after the date the Secretary receives a complete spend plan. It further permits the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, if requested, to review a completed spend plan concurrently with the Secretary, but expressly prohibits the Director from delaying the 90-day timeline for making funds available.

The Act does not authorize or appropriate new funds; it imposes procedural constraints on the administration of funds already available under the fishery resource disaster assistance program. No separate effective date is specified; the amendments took effect upon enactment on January 4, 2025.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Accelerating Appraisals and Conservation Efforts Act (AACE Act), Public Law 118-230, establishes a policy on appraisal and valuation services for real property in transactions under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of the Interior.

The bill's central provision allows a "covered appraiser" (a state-licensed or state-certified real property appraiser) to be licensed or certified in only one state in order to perform appraisal or valuation services for real property in any state, provided the work is for a transaction over which the Secretary of the Interior has jurisdiction. This changes prior law: any federal or state law enacted before this Act that requires an appraiser to be licensed in a specific state to work in that state no longer applies to such transactions. Outside of these transactions, existing licensing requirements continue to apply, and the Act does not otherwise alter the application of federal or state laws to non-federal appraisers.

When the Secretary uses a non-federal appraiser, the Secretary must, to the maximum extent practicable, use a certified general real property appraiser licensed in the state where the property is located. An appraiser licensed in another state may be used only if the Secretary determines that an in-state appraiser is unavailable within a reasonable time, not qualified for the assignment, or not cost competitive.

The Act requires the Secretary to submit a report to Congress within one year of enactment and annually for at least four more years. Each report must compare the number of appraisal requests and completion times before and after enactment, assess the impact of the new flexibility, offer recommendations, provide an overview of the Department's appraisal workforce, and list all cases where this authority was used and the criteria applied.

Within 90 days of enactment, the Department must make publicly available online all policies, manuals, guidance, handbooks, and procedures related to scoping, contracting, and reviewing appraisals.

The Act was approved January 4, 2025.

The Accelerating Appraisals and Conservation Efforts Act (AACE Act), Public Law 118-230, enacted January 4, 2025 (originating as H.R. 5443), establishes a federal policy governing appraisal and valuation services for real property in transactions over which the Secretary of the Interior has jurisdiction. Section 2 is codified at 43 U.S.C. 1478; Section 1 (short title) appears as a note to 43 U.S.C. 1451.

The Act's operative mechanism (Section 2(a)) provides that a "covered appraiser"—defined in subsection (f)(1) as a State-licensed or -certified real property appraiser—need be licensed or certified in only one State to perform appraisal or valuation services in any State for a transaction within the Secretary's jurisdiction, thereby overriding State-specific licensure requirements for such federal transactions.

Subsection (b) governs the Secretary's use of non-Federal covered appraisers. It directs the Secretary, to the maximum extent practicable, to use a certified general real property appraiser licensed in the State where the subject property is located (paragraph (1)), and permits use of an out-of-State appraiser only upon the Secretary's determination that an in-State appraiser is unavailable within a reasonable period, not assignment qualified, or not cost competitive (paragraph (2)).

Subsection (d) contains statutory clarifications. Paragraph (1) preserves the application of other Federal and State laws and regulations to non-Federal covered appraisers, "except as provided in paragraph (3)." anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "Think Differently About Emergencies Act" (Public Law 118-123), enacted November 25, 2024, directs the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to report to Congress and conduct a review concerning the assistance it provides to people with disabilities and their families affected by major disasters.

The Act has two main requirements. First, within 120 days of enactment, the FEMA Administrator must submit a report to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. The report must describe the assistance and resources FEMA provides—to states, localities, nonprofit organizations, and directly to individuals—for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their families who are impacted by major disasters declared under section 401 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act. The report must include the resources and best practices FEMA makes available, the process for training and deploying personnel to coordinate disaster assistance, the number of relevant FEMA programs (including those providing accommodations), FEMA's outreach to state, local, and nonprofit experts, and identified areas for improvement.

Second, within one year of enactment, both the Comptroller General of the United States and the FEMA Administrator must each conduct a review of the assistance and resources FEMA provides to states, localities, nonprofit organizations, and individuals to help people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, people with physical disabilities, and their families. Each review must identify potential legal impediments to providing such assistance, and provide Congress with recommendations on how FEMA can improve the assistance, enhance coordination with states, localities, and nonprofit organizations, and streamline the application and delivery process. Each must also recommend any legislative reforms needed.

The Act establishes reporting and review obligations only; it does not, by its terms, create new assistance programs or alter the substance of existing disaster relief law.

expert.summary:
Public Law 118-124, the "Fiscal Year 2024 Veterans Affairs Major Medical Facility Authorization Act" (enacted from H.R. 6324, approved November 25, 2024), authorizes the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to undertake a discrete set of enumerated major medical facility projects for fiscal year 2024 and authorizes appropriations to fund them.

Section 1 provides the short title. Section 2(a) confers project-specific authority: it permits the Secretary to carry out eleven identified major medical facility projects in FY2024, each at a specified location and subject to a per-project statutory ceiling ("in an amount . . . not to exceed"). The authorized projects, with their respective caps, are: American Lake, Washington ($155,600,000); Dallas, Texas ($93,100,000); El Paso, Texas ($759,200,000); Perry Point, Maryland ($274,310,000); Portland, Oregon ($613,000,000); Reno, Nevada (Sierra Nevada Health Care System replacement initiation, including land acquisition and preliminary site work — $223,800,000); San Diego, California ($311,700,000); San Francisco, California ($264,500,000); San Juan, Puerto Rico ($370,370,000); St. Louis, Missouri (Phase 1 — $135,340,000); and West Haven, Connecticut ($153,128,000). The scopes of work are project-specific and include new construction, renovation, seismic retrofit/corrections, parking expansion, utility plant work, land acquisition, and demolition, as detailed for each site.

This authorization operates within the statutory framework governing VA major medical facility projects under 38 U.S.C. Chapter 81 (notably 38 U.S.C. § 8104, which requires specific statutory authorization of major medical facility projects before funds may be obligated). The bill does not amend, repeal, or add new sections to the U.S. Code; it functions as freestanding project authorization legislation of the type contemplated by section 8104.

Section 2(b) is an authorization of appropriations, distinct from an appropriation. It authorizes to be appropriated to the Secretary $3,354,048,000 for the projects authorized in subsection (a), available for FY2024 "or the year in which funds are appropriated for the Construction, Major Projects account." This aggregate figure corresponds to the sum of the per-project ceilings. No budget authority is provided by this Act; actual funding requires a separate appropriation.

The Act contains no sunset provision, no separate effective-date provision (thus taking effect upon enactment), and no stated deadlines or conditions precedent beyond the per-project cost ceilings and the FY2024/year-of-appropriation availability limitation applicable to the authorized appropriations.

The Confirmation Of Congressional Observer Access Act of 2024 (COCOA Act of 2024) amends the Help America Vote Act of 2002 to require states to grant access to designated congressional election observers during federal elections.

The law adds a new Section 304 to Title III of the Help America Vote Act. It begins by stating Congress's position that, under Article I of the Constitution, it already has the authority to send observers to polling locations and any location where votes are processed, scanned, tabulated, canvassed, recounted, audited, or certified. The bill states that it does not establish new authorities but provides a statutory reference for existing congressional activity.

Under the new provision, states must give each designated congressional election observer full access to observe all elements of election administration, including areas where ballots are cast, processed, tabulated, recounted, audited, or certified, including pre- and post-election procedures. Observers may ask questions of election officials and workers.

The bill restricts observer conduct: observers may not handle ballots or election equipment, advocate for any candidate or position, reduce ballot secrecy or voter privacy, or interfere with voters or election administrators.

State or local election officials may remove an observer if they have a reasonable basis to believe the observer has engaged in or will imminently engage in intimidation, deceptive practices prohibited by federal law, or disruption of voting or ballot processing. The mere presence of an observer is not sufficient grounds for removal. If an observer is removed, the official must, within 24 hours, notify the chair and ranking minority member of the House Committee on House Administration or the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration and provide written reasons. The relevant committee leaders may send a replacement observer.

A "designated congressional election observer" is a House or Senate employee designated in writing by the chair or ranking minority member of the relevant committee. "State" includes the 50 states, the District of Columbia, and listed U.S. territories.

The Act also makes conforming enforcement and clerical amendments. It was approved October 4, 2024.

Public Law 118-106, the "Confirmation Of Congressional Observer Access Act of 2024" (or "COCOA Act of 2024"), amends Title III of the Help America Vote Act of 2002 (HAVA) (52 U.S.C. 21081 et seq.) to codify a statutory reference to Congress's asserted constitutional authority to send observers to federal elections and to impose an affirmative access requirement on States.

Section 2(a) restructures Title III by redesignating existing sections 304 and 305 (52 U.S.C. 21084, 21085) as sections 305 and 306, and inserting a new section 304 (codified as a note to 52 U.S.C. 21083a). Subsection (a) of new section 304 sets forth a congressional finding that, under Article I, Section 5, Clause 1 and Article I, Section 4, Clause 1 of the Constitution, Congress possesses authority to observe polling and vote-processing locations regardless of legislative action, and expressly disclaims creating any new authority or procedure, characterizing the provision as a convenient statutory reference to existing authority.

Subsection (b) requires each State to provide "designated congressional election observers" full access to observe all elements of election administration in federal elections, including areas where ballots are cast, processed, scanned, tabulated, canvassed, recounted, audited, or certified, during pre- and post-election procedures. Paragraph (2) restricts observers from handling ballots or equipment, advocating for positions or candidates, reducing ballot secrecy or voter privacy, or interfering with voting or administration. A rule of construction (paragraph (3)) preserves observers' ability to question officials.

Subsection (c) authorizes State or local election officials to remove an observer upon a "reasonable basis" to believe the observer has engaged in or imminently will engage in intimidation, deceptive practices prohibited by federal law, or disruption of election processes. A removing official must, within 24 hours, notify and provide written justification to the chair and ranking minority member of the Committee on House Administration or the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, as applicable. A rule of construction bars removal based on mere presence absent additional indicia. Upon proper removal, the relevant committee chair or ranking member may send a replacement observer for the remaining duration.

Subsection (d) defines a "designated congressional election observer" as a House or Senate employee designated in writing by the chair or ranking minority member of the named committees (or successor committees) to gather election information, including for contested-election purposes. Subsection (e) defines "State" to include the 50 States, D.C., Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands.

Section 2(b) makes a conforming amendment to HAVA section 401 (52 U.S.C. 21111), extending its enforcement mechanism to new section 304. Section 2(c) makes corresponding clerical amendments to the table of contents. The Act contains no appropriation, authorization of appropriations, sunset, or delayed effective date; it was approved October 4, 2024.

New section 304(a) states a finding that Congress possesses constitutional authority under Article I, section 5, clause 1 and Article I, section 4, clause 1 to send observers, and that the section’s procedures do not establish new authorities but provide a convenient statutory reference. Subsection (b) requires each State to give a designated congressional election observer “full access to clearly observe all elements of election administration procedures,” including access to any area where a ballot is cast, processed, scanned, tabulated, canvassed, recounted, audited, or certified, during pre- and post-election procedures. The observer may not handle ballots or election equipment, advocate for a position or candidate, reduce ballot secrecy or voter privacy, interfere with a voter or election administrator, or otherwise disrupt the process. Subsection (b)(3) clarifies that an observer may ask questions of election officials.

Subsection (c) governs removal. A state or local election official who has a reasonable basis to believe an observer has engaged in or imminently will engage in intimidation, deceptive practices prohibited by federal law, or disruption of voting, processing, scanning, tabulating, canvassing, recounting, or certification may remove the observer. The official must, within 24 hours, inform the chair and ranking minority member of the relevant congressional committee (the Committee on House Administration or the Committee on Rules and Administration) and provide written notice of the reasons for removal. Mere presence of an observer, without additional indicia, is not a sufficient basis for removal. If an observer is properly removed, the chair or ranking minority member may send a replacement observer for the remainder of the observation period.

Subsection (d) defines “designated congressional election observer” as a House or Senate employee designated in writing by the chair or ranking minority member of the Committee on House Administration or the Committee on Rules and Administration (or a successor committee) to gather information about an election, including for contested election purposes. Subsection (e) defines “State” to include the 50 States, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands.

The Act amends section 401 of HAVA (52 U.S.C. 21111) by adding “304” to the list of sections subject to the enforcement provision, thereby making the access requirement enforceable by the Attorney General. The Act contains no separate authorization of appropriations or delayed effective date; it took effect upon enactment on October 4, 2024.

The HEARTS Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-176) amends the Public Health Service Act to expand federal efforts on cardiomyopathy education, awareness, research, and the availability of automated external defibrillators (AEDs) and CPR training in schools. It adds four new sections (312A–312D) to the Act.

**Education materials (Section 312A):** Within 18 months of enactment, the Secretary of Health and Human Services, in consultation with the CDC Director, must develop public education materials covering: signs, symptoms, and risk factors of high-risk cardiac conditions (including cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, and others) that may cause sudden cardiac arrest in young people; guidelines for AED placement in schools and childcare settings; AED and CPR training information; and recommendations for cardiac emergency response plans. Within 30 months, the Secretary must disseminate these materials through state educational agencies, health departments, health professionals, and the CDC website.

**Cardiomyopathy activities (Section 312B):** Within 18 months, the Secretary, through the CDC, must report to Congress on existing findings about the prevalence and epidemiology of cardiomyopathy, including related emergency visits and hospitalizations. The report must be public while complying with privacy laws. The Secretary must also develop a publicly available cardiomyopathy risk assessment for providers and individuals, with input from patient advocacy groups, medical societies, and federal agencies.

**Research (Section 312C):** The Secretary, with the NIH Director, may expand and coordinate NIH research on cardiomyopathy causes, outcomes, and treatments, avoiding duplication of other HHS efforts. Within 18 months, a report to Congress must outline ongoing research and identify research agendas and areas of greatest need.

**School AED/CPR grants (Section 312D):** The Secretary may award grants to local educational agencies (in consultation with qualified health care entities) to promote student access to AEDs and CPR in public schools, funding training, materials, emergency plans, and the purchase and maintenance of approved AEDs.

The Act authorizes no additional appropriations to carry out these provisions. It was approved December 23, 2024.

Its purpose is to direct the development and dissemination of cardiomyopathy education, awareness, and risk-assessment materials; authorize related research and surveillance; and authorize a grant program for AED and CPR access in schools. New PHSA § 312B requires the Secretary, acting through the CDC Director, to submit to Congress within 18 months a report on existing CDC activities concerning cardiomyopathy prevalence and epidemiology (including natural history and estimates of emergency department visits and hospitalizations), to be made public subject to applicable federal and state privacy laws. The Congenital Heart Futures Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-107) amends Section 399V-2 of the Public Health Service Act to extend and expand the federal government's national program for congenital heart disease research, surveillance, and awareness.

The bill's primary purpose is to reauthorize this program and to require new reporting and strategic planning related to congenital heart disease.

The Act makes three main changes. First, it adds a new requirement for the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue a report to specified congressional committees (the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions) within two years of enactment. This report must describe past and present federal activities to raise public awareness of congenital heart disease, assess efforts to educate and train health care providers, and describe the current U.S. workforce capacity of providers treating adult patients with the disease.

Second, the bill requires the Secretary, within one year after submitting that report, to develop and submit to Congress a strategy for improving public awareness and provider education and training. The strategy must include findings and recommendations to address gaps in public awareness and research regarding patients' lifelong needs (including long-term outcomes, quality of life, mental health, and health care utilization), address shortages in the workforce treating adult patients (potentially through fellowship or continuing education programs), and foster collaboration across federal agencies, providers, researchers, and patient organizations. In developing the strategy, the Secretary is to consult, as appropriate, with stakeholder groups such as patient organizations, health care professionals, research entities, insurers, accrediting organizations, and federal agencies including the CDC, NIH, and HRSA.

Third, the bill extends the program's authorization of appropriations, replacing the prior period of fiscal years 2020 through 2024 with fiscal years 2025 through 2029. It also redesignates existing subsections (f) and (g) as (g) and (h).

The Act was approved on November 21, 2024.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The "Prove It Act of 2024" (H.R. 7198) amends Chapter 6 of title 5 of the U.S. Code to increase transparency in federal regulatory decisions affecting small businesses under the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

The bill expands the required content of an agency's initial regulatory flexibility analysis (Section 603(b)) to include, where feasible, reasonably foreseeable indirect costs a proposed rule may impose on small entities—such as those that do business with directly regulated entities, are regulated by other governmental bodies because of the rule, or become subject to other agency rules as a result.

It creates a new petition process (new Section 605A). When an agency certifies that a proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, small entities or organizations representing them may petition the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration to review that certification. Petitions must meet specified content requirements. Petitioners may request a consultation with the Chief Counsel, who is limited to procedural assistance and cannot advise on amending or withdrawing the petition.

The Chief Counsel conducts a prima facie review and, within 10 days, either closes the matter or proceeds to a full review. A full review involves examining the agency's analysis and convening a meeting with the petitioner, agency representatives, and the Administrator of OIRA; results must be published within 30 days. If the Chief Counsel finds a significant economic impact, the agency must perform initial and final regulatory flexibility analyses. If an agency fails to participate in the review, the final rule will not apply to small entities. Certain certifications are treated as final agency action for judicial review purposes.

The bill also requires agencies to publish guidance documents on regulations.gov and allow comment on them (Section 609). It expands periodic review of rules (Section 610) to include indirect costs, and provides that rules not reviewed within the required 10-year period cease to be effective unless reinstated after public comment and completed review within 180 days. This provision applies to final rules issued during the five years before enactment or afterward.

The bill passed the House on December 5, 2024.

The "Prove It Act of 2024" (H.R. 7198, 118th Congress), as passed by the House on December 5, 2024, and received in the Senate on December 9, 2024, amends Chapter 6 of title 5, U.S. Code (the Regulatory Flexibility Act), to expand small-entity impact disclosure requirements and create a new petition-and-review mechanism administered by the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration.

Section 2 amends § 603(b) to add a new paragraph (6) requiring each initial regulatory flexibility analysis, "where feasible," to identify reasonably foreseeable indirect costs on small entities, including entities transacting with directly regulated entities, entities regulated by other governmental bodies as a result of the rule, and entities subject to other agency rules as a result of the rule. It amends § 605(b) to impose a 10-day deadline (after certification) for the agency to publish a certification that a proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.

Section 2 also adds a new § 605A establishing a petition process. Any small entity, group, or representative organization may petition the Chief Counsel to review a § 605(b) certification; the section specifies petition form, content, and consultation procedures (with the Chief Counsel barred from advising whether to amend or withdraw). The Chief Counsel must conduct a prima facie review within 10 days: if the petition lacks merit, the matter is closed; if it merits review, the Chief Counsel notifies the petitioner and agency and undertakes a full review. Full review requires specified considerations, a mandatory meeting (including OIRA's Administrator), and publication of results in the Federal Register and on the Office of Advocacy website within 30 days. If the Chief Counsel determines a significant impact exists, the agency must perform initial and final regulatory flexibility analyses under §§ 603 and 604. As a penalty, if an agency fails to attend the required meeting or otherwise fails to assist, the final rule "shall not apply to small entities." For chapter 7 judicial review, the certification becomes final agency action upon a no-further-review determination or publication of full-review results.

Section 3 adds § 609(f), requiring agencies, for rules likely to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, to publish guidance and related documents on regulations.gov (or similar) and allow comment.

Section 4 amends § 610 to require periodic review to address indirect costs (new paragraph (6)) and adds subsection (d): if an agency fails to complete required 10-year review, the rule ceases to be effective, subject to a Federal Register notification, comment solicitation, and a 180-day reinstatement review (bypassing § 553 procedures). Petitions must include specified identifying information, alleged defects in the certification, supporting nonprotected or nonconfidential data, proposed solutions, and supporting analysis. The Chief Counsel must conduct an initial prima facie review and, within 10 days after receipt, either close the matter or notify the petitioner and agency that a full review will occur. expert.summary:
### Legislative Summary: Prove It Act of 2024 (H.R. 7198)

#### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism
The primary purpose of H.R. 7198 is to increase transparency, accountability, and administrative oversight regarding federal regulatory actions that impact small entities. The bill achieves this by amending Chapter 6 of Title 5, United States Code (commonly referred to as the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)), to expand the scope of required regulatory analyses, establish an administrative petition and review process overseen by the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the Small Business Administration (SBA) to challenge agency certifications, and impose automatic sunset penalties for non-compliance with periodic review requirements.

#### Major Provisions and Statutory Amendments

##### 1. Expansion of Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) Scope
Section 2(a)(1) amends 5 U.S.C. § 603(b) by adding a new paragraph (6). This provision requires agencies, where feasible, to include in their IRFA any reasonably foreseeable potential indirect costs a proposed rule may impose on small entities. This includes small entities that:
* Purchase from, sell to, or conduct business with directly regulated entities;
* Are directly regulated by other governmental entities as a result of the rule; or
* Are subject to other agency rules as a result of the rule.

##### 2. Agency Certification Timelines
Section 2(a)(2) amends 5 U.S.C. § 605(b) to establish a strict statutory deadline, requiring an agency to publish its certification that a rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities not later than 10 days after completing the certification.

##### 3. Administrative Petition and Review Process for Certifications
Section 2(a)(3) inserts a new section, 5 U.S.C. § 605A, establishing a multi-stage administrative review process for § 605(b) certifications:
* **Filing and Contents (§ 605A(a)):** Permits any small entity, group of small entities, or representative organization to petition the SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy to review a § 605(b) certification. The petition must meet specific pleading standards, including identifying information, specific assertions of incorrect or inadequate certification, supporting technical or scientific data, and proposed regulatory alternatives.
* **Consultation (§ 605A(b)):** Authorizes pre- or post-filing consultations between petitioners and the Chief Counsel, subject to statutory limitations prohibiting the Chief Counsel from advising on whether to amend or withdraw a petition.
* **Prima Facie Review (§ 605A(c)):** Mandates that the Chief Counsel make an initial determination on the merits of the petition within 10 days of receipt. If the petition lacks merit, the matter is closed. If it has merit, the Chief Counsel must notify the petitioner and the promulgating agency of a transition to full review.
* **Full Review (§ 605A(d)):** Establishes a 30-day timeline for the Chief Counsel to conduct a comprehensive review, which must include a virtual or in-person meeting with the petitioner, agency representatives, and the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA). Results must be published in the Federal Register and on the SBA Office of Advocacy website.
* **Operative Consequences and Penalties (§ 605A(d)(3)–(4)):** If the Chief Counsel determines the rule will have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, the agency *shall* perform an IRFA and a Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) under 5 U.S.C. §§ 603 and 604. If an agency fails to attend the mandatory meeting or assist in the review, the final rule shall not apply to small entities.
* **Judicial Review (§ 605A(d)(5)):** For the purposes of judicial review under 5 U.S.C. Chapter 7, a § 605(b) certification is deemed "final agency action" upon either the Chief Counsel's dismissal at the prima facie stage or the publication of the full review results.

##### 4. Publication of Guidance and Public Comment
Section 3 amends 5 U.S.C. § 609 by adding subsection (f), requiring agency heads to publish all guidance and interpretive documents for rules expected to have a significant economic impact on small entities on regulations.gov (or a similar website) and allow public comment on those documents.

##### 5. Periodic Review of Rules and Sunset Penalties
Section 4(a) amends 5 U.S.C. § 610. It adds 5 U.S.C. § 610(b)(6) to require agencies to consider indirect costs (as defined in § 603(b)(6)) during their 10-year periodic review of rules. 

Section 4(a)(2) adds 5 U.S.C. § 610(d), creating an automatic sunset mechanism:
* **Sunset Trigger:** If an agency fails to conduct the required § 610 review within the 10-year period, the Chief Counsel must notify the agency, and the rule automatically ceases to be effective. The agency must publish a notice of invalidity in the Federal Register and solicit comments regarding reinstatement.
* **Reinstatement Exception:** If the agency determines the rule should be reinstated, it has a 180-day deadline from that determination to complete the § 610 review. Upon completion, the rule is reinstated, notwithstanding the notice-and-comment requirements of 5 U.S.C. § 553.

#### Application and Effective Dates
The sunset and reinstatement provisions under the amended 5 U.S.C. § 610(d) apply retroactively to any final rule issued during the 5-year period preceding the date of enactment, as well as prospectively to any final rule issued on or after the date of enactment. No separate appropriations are authorized under this Act.

The Autism Collaboration, Accountability, Research, Education, and Support Act of 2024 (Autism CARES Act of 2024) amends the Public Health Service Act to reauthorize and expand federal activities and programs related to autism spectrum disorder (ASD). It became Public Law 118-180 on December 23, 2024.

**National Institutes of Health (NIH) activities.** The bill broadens the scope of autism research the NIH supports, adding fields such as psychiatry, psychology, developmental behavioral pediatrics, audiology, and gerontology. It directs that research address services and supports across the lifespan, examine supports for caregivers, and reflect the full population of individuals with ASD, including those with co-occurring conditions. It expands the number of authorized Centers of Excellence reviews, adds public input requirements, and requires the NIH Director to submit annual budget estimates for fiscal years 2026 through 2029 tied to the autism research strategic plan.

**Autism programs.** The bill extends the authorization of the developmental disabilities surveillance and research program, the autism education/early detection/intervention program, and the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee from December 20, 2024, to September 30, 2029. It replaces terms like "culturally competent" with "culturally and linguistically appropriate," and "at higher risk" with "at increased likelihood." It strengthens early-detection program capacity, requires a report within two years on expanding developmental-behavioral pediatrician training, and revises intervention research provisions to focus on evidence-based practices across the lifespan.

**Reports and committee.** The Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee must develop a strategic plan with budgetary requirements and submit annual and biennial updates. The bill requires updated reports to Congress, including a report on mental health needs of individuals with ASD and, within two years, an update on young adults transitioning from school-based services to adult services.

**Funding.** It raises authorized appropriations for fiscal years 2025–2029: to $28,100,000, $56,344,000, and $306,000,000 for the respective programs.

**Communication tools.** Section 4 authorizes the Secretary of Health and Human Services to provide training and technical assistance, upon request, to states, tribes, localities, or territories regarding using federal funding for communication-supporting services and technologies, with annual reports to Congress.

expert.summary:
### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism

The Autism Collaboration, Accountability, Research, Education, and Support Act of 2024 (Autism CARES Act of 2024), Public Law 118-180, amends the Public Health Service Act (PHSA) to reauthorize, expand, and modify federal research, surveillance, education, and intervention programs concerning autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and co-occurring conditions. The Act’s primary operative mechanisms are the extension of statutory sunsets, the authorization of increased appropriations for fiscal years (FY) 2025 through 2029, and the expansion of the scope of National Institutes of Health (NIH) and Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) programs to address the entire population of individuals with ASD across their lifespan.

---

### Major Provisions and Statutory Amendments

#### Section 2: National Institutes of Health Activities
*   **Expansion of Research Scope:** Section 2(a) amends PHSA § 409C(a)(1) (42 U.S.C. 284g(a)(1)) to mandate that the Director of NIH, in consultation with relevant federal departments and agencies, expand basic and clinical research. It adds psychiatry, psychology, developmental behavioral pediatrics, audiology, and gerontology to the enumerated fields of research. It further mandates that research investigate services and supports across the lifespan, co-occurring conditions, caregiver supports, and the safety and well-being of the entire ASD population.
*   **Centers of Excellence:** Section 2(b) amends PHSA § 409C(b) (42 U.S.C. 284g(b)) to add gerontology to the fields of research for Centers of Excellence and increases the maximum number of designated centers from five to seven.
*   **Public Input and Engagement Guidance:** Section 2(c) replaces PHSA § 409C(d) (42 U.S.C. 284g(d)) to require the NIH Director to provide public feedback mechanisms and authorizes the Director to issue guidance to Centers of Excellence on strategies to engage and solicit input from individuals with ASD, families, guardians, and advocates.
*   **Budget Estimate Mandate:** Section 2(d) adds PHSA § 409C(e) (42 U.S.C. 284g(e)), establishing a new statutory requirement for FY 2026 through FY 2029. The NIH Director must prepare and submit an annual budget estimate for NIH initiatives directly to the President for transmittal to Congress. This submission is subject to a comment period by the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee (IACC), but must be transmitted without change.

#### Section 3: Programs Relating to Autism
*   **Developmental Disabilities Surveillance and Research Program:** Section 3(a) amends PHSA § 399AA (42 U.S.C. 280i) to insert "across the lifespan" into the program's scope, make technical capitalization changes regarding Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations, and extend the program's statutory sunset from December 20, 2024, to September 30, 2029.
*   **Autism Education, Early Detection, and Intervention:** Section 3(b) amends PHSA § 399BB (42 U.S.C. 280i-1) to:
    *   Replace "culturally competent" with "culturally and linguistically appropriate" information requirements.
    *   Expand research promotion to include community-based approaches and diagnostic tools.
    *   Amend subsection (e)(1) to expand and strengthen the capacity of existing state developmental-behavioral pediatrician training programs, and establish new programs in states lacking them.
    *   Amend subsection (f) to direct the Secretary of HHS to promote research via grants or contracts to develop, evaluate, and disseminate evidence-based practices, interventions, and guidelines addressing physical, behavioral, and communication needs across the lifespan.
    *   Extend the program's statutory sunset to September 30, 2029.
*   **Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee (IACC):** Section 3(c) amends PHSA § 399CC (42 U.S.C. 280i-2) to require the IACC to meet on a regular basis. It replaces paragraphs (5) and (6) of subsection (b) to mandate that the IACC develop a strategic plan for ASD research containing proposed budgetary requirements and non-duplication recommendations. It also requires an annual update on the summary of advances and a biennial update on the strategic plan. The IACC's statutory sunset is extended to September 30, 2029.
*   **Reports to Congress:** Section 3(d) amends PHSA § 399DD (42 U.S.C. 280i-3) to:
    *   Require a progress report on ASD activities and research across the entire ASD population, to be submitted to Congress and posted publicly on the HHS website within four years of September 30, 2024.
    *   Refocus the report under subsection (b) from "Health and Well-Being" to "Mental Health Needs," requiring an overview of policies and recommendations to address mental health disparities and care coordination.
    *   Add subsection (c), requiring the Secretary of HHS to submit an update to Congress within two years of enactment regarding young adults transitioning from school-based services to adulthood.

---

### Authorizations of Appropriations, Conditions, and Deadlines

#### Section 3(e) Authorizations of Appropriations (FY 2025–2029)
The Act authorizes appropriations under PHSA § 399EE (42 U.S.C. 280i-4) as follows:
*   **PHSA § 399AA (Surveillance):** $28,100,000 authorized for each of fiscal years 2025 through 2029 (increased from $23,100,000).
*   **PHSA § 399BB (Education, Detection, Intervention):** $56,344,000 authorized for each of fiscal years 2025 through 2029 (increased from $50,599,000).
*   **NIH Activities (PHSA § 409C):** $306,000,000 authorized for each of fiscal years 2025 through 2029 (increased from $296,000,000).

#### Deadlines and Conditions Precedent
*   **Developmental-Behavioral Pediatrician Training Report:** Under amended PHSA § 399BB(e)(2)(C), the Secretary of HHS must submit a feasibility and needs report on expanding training programs to the Senate HELP Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee within two years of enactment (by December 23, 2026).
*   **Transitioning Youth Report Update:** Under PHSA § 399DD(c), the Secretary of HHS must submit the update on transitioning youth within two years of enactment (by December 23, 2026).
*   **Progress Report on ASD Activities:** Under PHSA § 399DD(a)(1), the progress report must be submitted and posted online within four years of September 30, 2024 (by September 30, 2028).

---

### Section 4: Technical Assistance to Improve Access to Communication Tools
Section 4 (codified as a note to 42 U.S.C. 280i) establishes a new, non-PHSA statutory authority. 

*   **Condition Precedent:** Upon request by a State, Indian Tribe, Tribal organization, locality, or territory, the Secretary of HHS is authorized to provide training and technical assistance regarding the utilization of federal funds to provide individuals with ASD and other developmental disabilities with access to evidence-based communication services, tools, and technologies.
*   **Reporting Mandate:** The Secretary must submit an annual report to the Senate HELP Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee summarizing the technical assistance provided and advancements made in communication technologies during the preceding fiscal year. No specific appropriation is authorized for Section 4.
