anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The BOLD Infrastructure for Alzheimer's Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-142) amends title III of the Public Health Service Act to extend funding for an existing federal program that promotes public health knowledge and awareness of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.

Specifically, the law amends Section 398B(e) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 280c-5(e)) by adding an authorization of $33,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2025 through 2029. This continues funding for the program established under the original BOLD (Building Our Largest Dementia) Infrastructure for Alzheimer's framework.

The Act was approved on December 11, 2024. It originated as H.R. 7218, was passed by the House on September 17, 2024, and by the Senate on November 20, 2024.

The bill makes no other substantive changes to the underlying program's structure or operation; its sole effect is to extend and set the funding authorization level for the specified five-year period.

bills.title: Utah State Parks Adjustment Act

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Utah State Parks Adjustment Act (Public Law 118-181), enacted December 23, 2024, requires the federal government to transfer certain federal lands to the State of Utah for inclusion in three state parks.

The Act directs three conveyances, each to occur within 180 days of enactment, made subject to valid existing rights, without payment (no consideration), and by quitclaim deed:

1. **Antelope Island State Park:** The Secretary of the Interior must convey Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land identified on a map dated February 28, 2023.

2. **Wasatch Mountain State Park:** The Secretary of the Interior must convey BLM land identified on a map dated May 3, 2024.

3. **Fremont Indian State Park:** The Secretary of Agriculture must convey National Forest System land identified on a map dated September 12, 2023, along with any improvements on that land.

For all three conveyances, Utah must pay the associated costs, including surveys and other administrative expenses.

The Fremont Indian conveyance carries additional conditions. The Secretary of Agriculture must reserve easements for all National Forest System roads and trails that originate at, terminate at, or cross the conveyed land. The Secretary must convey only three specified water rights (numbered 63-44, 63-1607, and 63-2817) that serve the Castle Rock Campground and the Belknap Historic Guard Station interpretive site. If deemed necessary, the exact acreage and legal description will be set by a survey approved by the Secretary, with the State paying reasonable survey costs. The Secretary of Agriculture may enter agreements with the State on further terms, such as managing the Belknap site, roads and trails, continued livestock grazing, Forest Service access to retained water rights, and other management matters.

Either Secretary may make minor modifications to the applicable maps. The State must use all conveyed land for public purposes—including parks, campgrounds, recreation, and permitted livestock grazing. If any parcel ceases to be used for such purposes, it may, at the relevant Secretary's discretion, revert to the United States.

expert.summary:
Public Law 118-181, the "Utah State Parks Adjustment Act" (H.R. 7332), enacted December 23, 2024, directs the Secretary of the Interior and the Secretary of Agriculture to convey specified federal land to the State of Utah for inclusion in three designated state parks. The Act operates through mandatory, no-consideration quitclaim conveyances subject to valid existing rights.

Section 2(a) requires the Secretary of the Interior, not later than 180 days after enactment, to convey all right, title, and interest of the United States in Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land identified for conveyance on the map titled "Antelope Island State Park Proposal: Utah State Park Additions" (dated February 28, 2023), for inclusion in Antelope Island State Park. The State bears all costs, including survey and administrative costs.

Section 2(b) imposes a parallel 180-day mandatory conveyance obligation on the Secretary of the Interior for BLM land identified on the map titled "Wasatch Mountain State Park Proposal Utah State Park Additions" (dated May 3, 2024), for inclusion in Wasatch Mountain State Park, with costs likewise borne by the State.

Section 2(c) requires the Secretary of Agriculture, within 180 days, to convey National Forest System land identified on the map titled "S. 2136—Utah State Parks Adjustment Act" (dated September 12, 2023), together with any improvements, for inclusion in Fremont Indian State Park. This conveyance carries several conditions: (1) the Secretary must reserve easements for all National Forest System roads and trails originating at, terminating at, or traversing the conveyed land (§2(c)(2)); (2) the Secretary shall convey only the specified water rights (Utah State Engineer database identifiers 63-44, 63-1607, and 63-2817) serving the Castle Rock Campground and Belknap Historic Guard Station interpretive site (§2(c)(3)); (3) the State shall pay reasonable costs of any survey the Secretary determines necessary to establish exact acreage and legal description (§2(c)(4)). Section 2(c)(5) grants the Secretary discretionary authority to enter into an agreement with the State on additional terms, including management of the Belknap site, road/trail use, continued permitted livestock grazing, Forest Service access to retained water rights, and other management-clarifying terms.

Section 2(d) authorizes either Secretary to make minor modifications to the applicable maps, including changes reflecting surveys.

Section 2(e) requires the State to use conveyed land for public purposes (parks, campgrounds, recreation, permitted livestock grazing) and establishes a reversionary interest: if a conveyed parcel ceases such use, it may, at the applicable Secretary's discretion, revert to the United States.

The Act contains no appropriations.

The Royalty Resiliency Act (Public Law 118-81) amends Section 111(j) of the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982 to revise how the federal government manages royalties from oil and gas production under "units" and "communitization agreements" (arrangements that combine multiple leases or tracts for joint development).

The primary purpose is to establish a deadline for the Secretary of the Interior to determine how production is allocated among the parties in these agreements and to clarify how royalties are reported and paid while a determination is pending.

Under the revised provision, the Secretary must issue all determinations of production allocation for units and communitization agreements within 120 days of receiving a request. Until the Secretary issues a determination, the lessee (or its designee) must report and pay royalties on oil and gas production each month based on the terms of the proposed allocation. After the determination is issued, the lessee must correct any prior reports and royalty payments as necessary, completing those corrections no later than the end of the third month following the month in which it receives the determination.

The Act also addresses interest charges. Provided that royalties are paid fully and on time each month according to the proposed allocation, the Secretary must waive any interest otherwise due on the obligations covered by the determination, through the end of the third month following the month the lessee receives the determination.

The provision does not apply to unit or communitization agreements that contain Indian lands.

The Act was approved on September 20, 2024.

The government (led by the Secretary, a top official) must decide these allocations within 120 days after someone asks. That means about four months.

While the government is still deciding, companies must keep paying their royalties every month. They pay based on the plan they proposed.

After the government makes its decision, companies must fix their reports and payments if needed. They have until the end of the third month after they get the answer.

The law also talks about "interest." Interest is extra money you owe when a payment is late. If companies pay their monthly royalties fully and on time, the government will not charge them this extra interest. This break lasts until the end of the third month after they get the decision.

One important rule: this law does not apply to agreements that include Indian lands.

expert.summary:
Public Law 118-81, the "Royalty Resiliency Act" (H.R. 7377), enacted September 20, 2024, amends the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982 to establish procedures governing the interim reporting and payment of royalties pending the Secretary's determination of production allocations for units and communitization agreements.

Section 1 provides the short title. Section 2 amends Section 111(j) of the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982 (30 U.S.C. 1721(j))—as previously amended by the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Simplification and Fairness Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-185)—by striking the existing subsection and substituting new text.

As amended, Section 111(j) imposes on the Secretary a deadline requiring issuance of all determinations of allocations of production for units and communitization agreements within 120 days of a request for determination. Pending that determination, the operative mechanism directs that the lessee or its designee of a lease within a unit or communitization agreement report and pay royalties on oil and gas production for each production month in accordance with the terms of the proposed allocation of production.

Following issuance of the determination, the lessee or designee must, as necessary, correct such reports and the amount of royalties paid, with a correction deadline of no later than the end of the third month following the month in which the determination is received from the Secretary.

The amendment includes an interest-waiver provision: subject to the condition precedent of full and timely monthly payment of royalties to all parties in accordance with the terms of the proposed allocation, the Secretary shall waive interest due on obligations subject to the determination until the end of the third month following the month in which the lessee or designee receives the determination.

The subsection contains an express exception providing that it shall not apply to unit or communitization agreements containing Indian lands.

The Act contains no authorization of appropriations, no appropriation, and no sunset provision. No separate effective date is specified; accordingly, the amendment takes effect upon enactment. Section 1 is designated as a note to 30 U.S.C. 1701.

Once the Secretary issues the determination, the lessee or its designee must correct any necessary reports and adjust the amount of royalties paid by the end of the third month following the month they receive the determination.

Subject to the full and timely monthly payment of royalties to all parties according to the proposed allocation, the Secretary shall waive interest due on obligations subject to the determination until the end of the third month following the receipt of the determination. 

A material exception is provided: these new requirements do not apply to unit or communitization agreements that contain Indian lands. The Act was approved and became effective on September 20, 2024.

eli5.summary:
This law is called the Royalty Resiliency Act. It changes the rules for how the government manages money from oil and gas drilling on public land.

When companies drill for oil and gas, they often share the land and the profits. They must pay a share of the money, called a royalty, to the government. Sometimes, they need the government to decide exactly how to split the oil, gas, and money. This law says the government official in charge, called the Secretary, must make this decision within 120 days after a company asks.

While waiting for the decision, the company must keep paying the government based on a proposed plan. Once the Secretary makes the final decision, the company has three months to fix their reports and payments if they need to.

If the company pays on time using the proposed plan, the government will not charge them extra fees, called interest, while they wait. Finally, these new rules do not apply to agreements that include Indian lands.

expert.summary:
Public Law 118-81, cited as the "Royalty Resiliency Act," amends the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982 to improve the management of royalties from oil and gas leases. The Act's operative mechanism imposes a statutory deadline and an interim payment framework for the Secretary's determinations of allocations of production for units and communitization agreements.

Specifically, Section 2 amends Section 111(j) of the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982 (30 U.S.C. 1721(j)), as previously amended by the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Simplification and Fairness Act of 1996 (Public Law 104-185), to require the Secretary to issue all determinations of allocations of production for units and communitization agreements within 120 days of a request. Pending the Secretary's determination, the lessee or its designee must report and pay royalties on oil and gas production for each production month in accordance with the terms of the proposed allocation. Upon issuance of the determination, the lessee or its designee must correct such reports and royalty payments by no later than the end of the third month following the month in which the determination is received from the Secretary.

The amendment provides for a conditional waiver of interest. Subject to the full and timely monthly payment of royalties to all parties in accordance with the terms of the proposed allocation, the Secretary shall waive interest due on obligations subject to the determination until the end of the third month following the month in which the lessee or its designee receives the determination. 

The amendment contains a material exception, providing that the subsection shall not apply to unit or communitization agreements containing Indian lands. The Act does not include any authorizations or appropriations of funds. The Act was approved on September 20, 2024, and applies upon enactment.

This bill creates a faster process for oil and gas companies that drill on federal land. When several companies share a drilling area, they must agree on how to split the oil or gas they produce. This agreement is called an allocation. The government must approve this split so each company pays the correct royalties, which are payments to the government for using the land.

Right now, getting that government approval can take a long time. This bill sets a firm deadline: the government must make its decision within 120 days after a company asks for it. While waiting for the decision, the company will pay royalties based on its own proposed split. Once the government makes its final decision, the company has until the end of the third month after receiving it to fix any reports or payments if needed.

If the company has been paying on time each month based on its proposal, the government will not charge extra interest on any corrected amounts during that waiting and correction period. These new rules do not apply to drilling agreements that include Native American lands.

The Royalty Resiliency Act (Public Law 118-81) amends section 111(j) of the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982 (30 U.S.C. § 1721(j)) by striking the existing text—as previously amended by the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Simplification and Fairness Act of 1996 (Public Law 104-185)—and inserting a new subsection (j). The amendment establishes a mandatory deadline for the Secretary of the Interior to issue determinations of allocations of production for units and communitization agreements, prescribes an interim royalty reporting and payment rule, and provides a conditional interest waiver.

Specifically, new subsection (j) requires the Secretary to issue all such allocation determinations within 120 days of a request for determination. Until the Secretary issues the determination, the lessee or its designee shall report and pay royalties on oil and gas production for each production month in accordance with the terms of the proposed allocation of production for the unit or communitization agreement. Following the Secretary’s determination, the lessee or its designee shall, as necessary, correct those reports and royalty amounts by no later than the end of the third month following the month in which the determination is received. Subject to the condition that the lessee made full and timely monthly royalty payments to all parties consistent with the proposed allocation, the Secretary shall waive interest due on obligations subject to the determination until the end of that same correction period (i.e., the end of the third month following the month of receipt of the determination). The new subsection explicitly excludes from its application any unit or communitization agreements that contain Indian lands.

The Act contains no new authorization of appropriations, no sunset provision, and no retroactive application beyond the immediate effect of the statutory amendment. It took effect upon enactment on September 20, 2024.

crs_reference.summary:
Royalty Resiliency Act
This act modifies the process under which oil and gas leaseholders who have entered into certain joint drilling agreements (i.e., a communitization agreement or a unit agreement, except agreements containing Indian lands) to drill wells on leased land pay royalties to the Department of the Interior under the Federal Oil and Gas Royalty Management Act of 1982.
Under current law, Interior must issue a determination of allocations of royalty payments for oil and gas production under a joint agreement within 120 days of a request for determination. Generally, the first leaseholder to drill must pay any royalties due to Interior for all oil and gas production on the land subject to the agreement until Interior determines the royalty allocations of each leaseholder. If Interior fails to issue the determination by that deadline, then it must waive interest due on royalty obligations until the end of the month following the month in which the determination was made.
Under the act, a leaseholder must pay royalties on oil and gas production based on the lessee's proposed allocation of production under the joint agreement until Interior issues a determination of royalty allocations. After Interior issues the determination, then the lessee must correct, if necessary, the amount of royalties paid by the end of the third month following the month in which the lessee received the determination from Interior. Subject to the full and timely payment of monthly royalties in accordance with the agreement, Interior must waive interest due on royalty obligations until the end of the third month.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-41) is a short-term measure that extends expiring Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) authorizations, aviation-related funding, and certain taxes. Its primary purpose is to continue these programs for a brief period—generally through May 10 or May 11, 2024—pending longer-term reauthorization. Most provisions accomplish this by replacing prior expiration dates (commonly March 8 or March 9, 2024) with the new dates.

Title I addresses FAA programs. It authorizes approximately $2.04 billion for the airport improvement program for the period from October 1, 2023, through May 10, 2024, with obligation authority extending through September 30, 2024. For calculating funding apportionments during this period, the FAA Administrator must first compute amounts on an annualized basis as if $3.35 billion were available for fiscal year 2024, then reduce all apportionments and certain other amounts by 39 percent. Title I also extends project grant authority and numerous other authorities, including insurance authority, unmanned aircraft (UAS) test ranges and special UAS authorities, airport safety provisions, weather reporting programs, remote tower and other pilot programs, and various advisory committees. It sets new funding levels for FAA operations (about $7.26 billion), facilities and equipment (about $1.79 billion), research and development (about $155 million), and small community air service programs, including Essential Air Service (about $216 million).

Title II extends, through May 11, 2024, the authority to make expenditures from the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, and extends through May 10 or May 11, 2024, the taxes that fund it, including aviation fuel taxes, ticket taxes on persons and property, and taxes related to fractional ownership programs.

Title III extends, through May 11, 2024, counter-UAS authorities under the Homeland Security Act of 2002.

The Act was approved on March 8, 2024.

This law is called the "Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2024." Its main job is to keep money and rules flowing for airports and air travel for a little longer.

Here's the big idea. Many airport programs were set to end on March 8, 2024. This law pushes many of those end dates to May 10 or May 11, 2024. So it gives everyone more time before Congress makes a bigger, longer plan.

- About $2 billion to help fix and improve airports.
- About $7.2 billion to run the Federal Aviation Administration (the FAA is the group in charge of air travel safety).
- Money to help small towns keep their airplane service.
- Money for weather reporting and airport safety research.

expert.summary:
The Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2024 (Pub. L. 118-41, H.R. 7454, enacted March 8, 2024) is a short-term reauthorization measure that extends expiring Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) program authorities and Airport and Airway Trust Fund financing provisions through, in most cases, May 10 or May 11, 2024, primarily by amending title 49, United States Code, and the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. The bill operates almost exclusively through date-substitution amendments and revised interim authorization figures for the period beginning October 1, 2023.

Title I addresses FAA programs. Section 101 amends 49 U.S.C. 48103(a) to authorize $2,041,120,218 for the airport improvement program (AIP) through May 10, 2024; obligation authority runs through September 30, 2024, subject to advance appropriations limitations. Section 101(c) prescribes an apportionment methodology under 49 U.S.C. 47114–47117: apportionments are first calculated on an annualized $3,350,000,000 basis, then reduced by 39 percent. Sections 101(d)–(e) extend project grant authority (47104(c)) and the special apportionment rule (47114(c)(1)(J)) to May 10, 2024.

Section 102 extends numerous expiring authorities to May 10 or May 11, 2024, including war-risk insurance (44310(b)), UAS test ranges (44803(h)), special UAS authority (44807(d)), airspace hazard mitigation (44810(h)), and various pilot programs and advisory committees under the Vision 100 Act, the FAA Modernization and Reform Act of 2012, the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, and the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018. It sets revised interim authorization amounts for supplemental discretionary funds (47115(j)(4)(A): $340,321,762) and weather reporting programs (48105: $23,762,295).

Sections 103–105 revise interim authorizations: FAA operations under 49 U.S.C. 106(k) ($7,259,685,792); facilities and equipment under 48101(a) ($1,794,357,923); and research, engineering, and development under 48102(a) ($155,368,852), each for the period ending May 10, 2024. Section 106 raises Essential Air Service authorization (41742(a)(2)) to $216,192,407 and airports-not-receiving-sufficient-service funding (41743(e)(2)) to $6,092,896.

Title II extends Trust Fund financing. Section 201 amends I.R.C. § 9502(d)(1) and (e)(2) to extend expenditure authority to May 11, 2024, adding this Act to the enumerated authorizing statutes. Section 202 extends the aviation excise taxes funding the Trust Fund—fuel taxes (§ 4081(d)(2)(B)), ticket taxes on persons and property (§§ 4261(k), 4271(d)), and fractional-ownership-program provisions (§§ 4043(d), 4083(b), 4261(j))—to May 10 or May 11, 2024.

Title III, Section 301, extends counter-UAS authorities under section 210G(i) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 124n(i)) to May 11, 2024.

These provisions constitute authorizations, not appropriations.

expert.summary:
The *Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2024* (Pub. L. 118-41) is a short-term reauthorization statute designed to extend federal aviation programs, funding mechanisms, and related tax authorities through May 10, 2024, or May 11, 2024. 

### Title I: Federal Aviation Programs
Title I extends authorizations of appropriations and program authorities under Title 49 of the United States Code:
*   **Airport Improvement Program (AIP):** Section 101(a) amends 49 U.S.C. § 48103(a) to authorize $2,041,120,218 for the period from October 1, 2023, through May 10, 2024. Section 101(b) provides that this obligation authority is subject to advance appropriation limitations, may be obligated through September 30, 2024, and remains available until expended. Section 101(c) directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator to calculate apportionments under 49 U.S.C. §§ 47114–47117 on an annualized baseline of $3,350,000,000, and then apply a 39 percent reduction. Sections 101(d) and (e) extend AIP project grant authority (49 U.S.C. § 47104(c)) and the special rule for apportionments (49 U.S.C. § 47114(c)(1)(J)) through May 10, 2024.
*   **FAA Operations and Facilities:** Section 103 amends 49 U.S.C. § 106(k) to authorize $7,259,685,792 for FAA operations for the October 1, 2023–May 10, 2024 period, and extends general operational authority under § 106(k)(3) to May 10, 2024. Section 104 amends 49 U.S.C. § 48101(a) to authorize $1,794,357,923 for air navigation facilities and equipment. Section 105 amends 49 U.S.C. § 48102(a) to authorize $155,368,852 for research, engineering, and development.
*   **Small Community Air Service:** Section 106(a) amends 49 U.S.C. § 41742(a)(2) to increase the Essential Air Service authorization to $216,192,407 for the period ending May 10, 2024. Section 106(b) amends 49 U.S.C. § 41743(e)(2) to increase the authorization for communities deemed not to be receiving sufficient service to $6,092,896 for the same period.
*   **Expiring Authorities and Miscellaneous Extensions:** Section 102 extends various statutory deadlines and program authorizations from March 8, 2024 (or March 9, 2024), to May 10, 2024 (or May 11, 2024). Affected provisions include aviation insurance authority (49 U.S.C. § 44310(b)), unmanned aircraft test ranges (49 U.S.C. § 44803(h)), special UAS authority (49 U.S.C. § 44807(d)), airport safety and airspace hazard mitigation (49 U.S.C. § 44810(h)), competitive access reporting (49 U.S.C. § 47107(r)(3)), discretionary fund eligibility for the Marshall Islands, Micronesia, and Palau (49 U.S.C. § 47115(i)), compatible land use planning (49 U.S.C. § 47141(f)), and commercial space flight learning periods (51 U.S.C. § 50905(c)(9)). Section 102(g) authorizes $340,321,762 for supplemental discretionary funds under 49 U.S.C. § 47115(j)(4)(A), and Section 102(j) authorizes $23,762,295 for weather reporting programs under 49 U.S.C. § 48105.

### Title II: Aviation Revenue Provisions
Title II amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (IRC) to maintain the solvency and funding of the Airport and Airway Trust Fund:
*   **Expenditure Authority:** Section 201 amends IRC § 9502(d)(1) and § 9502(e)(2) to extend the trust fund's expenditure authority through May 11, 2024, making the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2024 a qualifying authorizing statute.
*   **Tax Extensions:** Section 202 extends excise taxes dedicated to the trust fund through May 10, 2024. This includes fuel taxes under IRC § 4081(d)(2)(B), ticket taxes on persons under IRC § 4261(k)(1)(A)(ii), and property transportation taxes under IRC § 4271(d)(1)(A)(ii). For fractional ownership programs, the fuel tax under IRC § 4043(d) and ticket tax exemptions under IRC § 4261(j) are extended through May 10, 2024, while treatment as noncommercial aviation under IRC § 4083(b) is extended through May 11, 2024.

Additionally, the legislation extends the Department of Homeland Security’s counter-unmanned aircraft systems (Counter-UAS) authorities.

Section 101(a) amends 49 U.S.C. § 48103(a) to authorize appropriations for the Airport Improvement Program (AIP) at $2,041,120,218 for October 1, 2023, through May 10, 2024. Sections 101(d) and (e) extend project grant authority under 49 U.S.C. § 47104(c) and the special apportionment rule under 49 U.S.C. § 47114(c)(1)(J) by replacing “March 8, 2024” with “May 10, 2024.”

crs_reference.label: CRS (human)
crs_reference.summary:
Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2024
This act temporarily extends specific Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) programs and activities through May 10, 2024.
TITLE I--FEDERAL AVIATION PROGRAMS
(Sec. 101) This section extends through May 10, 2024, the Airport Improvement Program (AIP). This program provides grants for planning, development, and noise compatibility projects at or associated with certain public-use airports.
(Sec. 102) This section extends through May 10, 2024, certain expiring Department of Transportation (DOT) and FAA authorities and programs.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority of DOT to provide insurance and reinsurance for the federal government for risks from operating an aircraft and providing related goods or services.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the FAA's Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Test Site Program, which provides verification of the safety of public and civil UAS, operations, and related navigation procedures before their integration into the national airspace system.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority of DOT to provide exemptions from some requirements for UAS by using a risk-based approach to determine if certain UAS may operate safely in the national airspace system.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the FAA's airport safety and airspace hazard mitigation and enforcement program to test and evaluate technologies or systems that detect and mitigate potential aviation safety risks posed by UAS.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, competitive access disclosure requirements for AIP grant applications for large and medium hub airports. Specifically, an airport must provide assurances to DOT that it will report if it has been unable to accommodate one or more requests by an air carrier for access to gates or other facilities at that airport in order to provide service or expanded service.
This section extends authorization through May 10, 2024, for AIP grants for airports located in the Republic of the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, and the Republic of Palau.
This section extends authorization through May 10, 2024, for the FAA AIP supplementary discretionary funds for grants for airport or terminal development projects.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, AIP grant authorization for compatible land use planning and projects by state and local governments. Airport-compatible land uses are those that can coexist with a nearby airport without constraining the safe and efficient operation of the airport, or exposing people living or working nearby to significant environmental impacts.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, authorization for the AIP non-movement area surveillance surface display systems pilot grant program. These systems use on-airport sensors to track vehicles or aircraft that are equipped with transponders on portions of the airfield surface that are not under the control of air traffic control.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, authorization for the FAA weather reporting programs.
This section extends to May 11, 2024, a learning period (i.e., moratorium) that applies to certain DOT commercial spaceflight safety regulations governing the design or operation of a launch vehicle to protect the health and safety of crew, government astronauts, and space flight participants.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, authority for DOT to enter into a reimbursable agreement with the Department of Interior for the purpose of funding airport development at Midway Island Airport.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the termination date for a final order establishing mileage and adjustment eligibility under the Essential Air Service (EAS) Program using the most commonly used route between the place and the nearest medium hub airport or large hub airport. (The EAS program was established to ensure that small communities that were served by certificated air carriers before the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 would continue to receive scheduled passenger service.)
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the moratorium on discontinuing the FAA Contract Weather Observer Program at any airport.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority for the FAA remote tower pilot program. A remote tower is a remotely operated air navigation facility, including all necessary system components, that provides the functions and capabilities of an air traffic control tower whereby air traffic services are provided to operators at an airport from a location that may not be on or near the airport.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority for DOT to provide AIP grants for airport access roads in certain remote locations and for storage facilities for certain snow removal and safety equipment.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority for the FAA's UAS remote detection and identification pilot program. Under the program, the FAA uses available remote detection or identification technologies for safety oversight, including enforcement actions against operators of UAS that are not in compliance with federal aviation laws and regulations.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority for the Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee, which advises DOT in carrying out activities relating to airline customer service improvements.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the requirement that the Aviation Consumer Advocate at DOT submit an annual report to Congress summarizing aviation consumer complaints and recommendations.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority for the FAA Air Carrier Access Act Advisory Committee to address the needs of passengers with disabilities.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority for an FAA pilot program to provide air traffic control services on a preferential basis to aircraft equipped with certain Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen) avionics.
This section extends through May 10, 2024, the pilot program that allows AIP funds to be used for activities related to the redevelopment of airport properties.
(Sec. 103) This section reauthorizes through May 10, 2024, FAA salaries, operations, and maintenance.
Further, this section extends through May 10, 2024, DOT's authority to reduce the FAA's expenses for non-safety-related activities if DOT determines that the funding levels are insufficient to meet the FAA's authorized salary, operations, and maintenance expenses.
(Sec. 104) This section extends through May 10, 2024, the FAA's authority to acquire, establish, and improve air navigation facilities and equipment.
(Sec. 105) This section extends through May 10, 2024, the FAA's authority to conduct civil aviation research, engineering, and development.
(Sec. 106) This section reauthorizes through May 10, 2024, the FAA Essential Air Service Program.
Further, this section reauthorizes through May 10, 2024, the Small Community Air Service Development Program, a DOT grant program designed to help small communities address air service and airfare issues.
TITLE II--AVIATION REVENUE PROVISIONS
(Sec. 201) This section extends through May 10, 2024, the FAA's authority for expenditures from the Airport and Airway Trust Fund (AATF). The AATF is the primary funding source for all major FAA accounts that fund federal aviation programs, with the remainder coming from general fund appropriations.
(Sec. 202) This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority for the FAA to collect various taxes and fees to fund the AATF, including taxes on aviation fuel and airline tickets.
TITLE III--MISCELLANEOUS EXTENSIONS
(Sec. 301) This section extends through May 10, 2024, the authority of the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to take certain actions to mitigate a credible threat to certain facilities or assets from an unmanned aircraft system (UAS). These include certain facilities that are located in the United States and identified as high-risk and a potential target for unlawful UAS activity.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-130) directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to increase the rates of certain benefits paid to veterans with service-connected disabilities and to survivors of certain disabled veterans, effective December 1, 2024.

The bill requires the Secretary to raise the dollar amounts that were in effect on November 30, 2024, for the following benefits:
- Wartime disability compensation (under section 1114 of title 38, U.S. Code);
- Additional compensation for dependents (section 1115(1));
- The clothing allowance (section 1162);
- Dependency and indemnity compensation paid to surviving spouses (section 1311, subsections (a) through (d)); and
- Dependency and indemnity compensation paid to children (sections 1313(a) and 1314).

The size of the increase is tied to the cost-of-living adjustment applied to Social Security benefits. Specifically, each covered amount is to be increased by the same percentage as the increase in Social Security benefits under title II of the Social Security Act that takes effect December 1, 2024, as determined under section 215(i) of that Act.

The Act also permits the Secretary to administratively adjust, consistent with these increases, the disability compensation rates payable to certain persons under section 10 of Public Law 85-857 who have not received compensation under chapter 11 of title 38.

The Secretary is required to publish the adjusted amounts in the Federal Register no later than the date by which the corresponding Social Security cost-of-living figures must be published for fiscal year 2025.

The law does not specify a fixed percentage increase itself; it links the increase to the Social Security adjustment. It was approved November 25, 2024.

The main thing this law does is make these payments bigger. This is called a cost-of-living adjustment. That means the money goes up so it keeps up with rising prices. When things cost more, the payments go up too.

The new, higher amounts start on December 1, 2024.

How much bigger will the payments be? They will go up by the same amount that Social Security payments go up. Social Security is money the government pays to older people and some others. So if Social Security goes up a certain amount, veterans' payments go up that same amount.

expert.summary:
Public Law 118-130, the "Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2024" (enacted November 25, 2024, from H.R. 7777), directs a cost-of-living increase in the rates of veterans' disability compensation and dependency and indemnity compensation (DIC), effective December 1, 2024.

Section 1 provides the short title (codified as a note to 38 U.S.C. 101).

Section 2(a) (set out as a note to 38 U.S.C. 1114) requires the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to increase, effective December 1, 2024, the dollar amounts in effect on November 30, 2024, for payment of disability compensation and DIC under the provisions enumerated in subsection (b), in accordance with the method prescribed in subsection (c).

Section 2(b) specifies the amounts subject to increase: (1) each dollar amount for wartime disability compensation under 38 U.S.C. 1114; (2) each dollar amount for additional compensation for dependents under 38 U.S.C. 1115(1); (3) the clothing allowance under 38 U.S.C. 1162; (4) each dollar amount for DIC to surviving spouses under subsections (a) through (d) of 38 U.S.C. 1311; and (5) each dollar amount for DIC to children under 38 U.S.C. 1313(a) and 1314.

Section 2(c) prescribes the mechanism for the increase: each enumerated amount is to be increased by the same percentage as the increase in Social Security benefit amounts payable under Title II of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 401 et seq.) effective December 1, 2024, as determined under section 215(i) of that Act (42 U.S.C. 415(i)). The COLA is thus tethered to the Social Security automatic-adjustment determination rather than fixed by a statutorily stated percentage.

Section 2(d) (also a note to 38 U.S.C. 1114) authorizes the Secretary to administratively adjust, consistent with the subsection (a) increases, the rates of disability compensation payable to persons under section 10 of Public Law 85-857 (72 Stat. 1263) who have not received compensation under chapter 11 of title 38.

Section 3 (a note to 38 U.S.C. 1114) requires the Secretary to publish in the Federal Register the amounts specified in section 2(b), as increased, not later than the date on which the corresponding Social Security matters under section 215(i)(2)(D) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 415(i)(2)(D)) must be published pursuant to a section 215(i) determination made during fiscal year 2025.

The Act amends no statutory text directly, operating through freestanding directives set out as statutory notes; it contains no appropriation and no sunset provision.

expert.summary:
The "Police Our Border Act" (H.R. 8146, 118th Congress) is a single-purpose reporting bill directing the Attorney General to submit one report to Congress concerning the asserted impact of border conditions on Federal, State, local, and Tribal law enforcement. As passed by the House on May 16, 2024, and received in the Senate and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on May 20, 2024, the bill contains no amendments to existing statute, no appropriation, and no authorization of appropriations.

Section 1 provides the short title. Section 2 sets forth congressional findings, including references to line-of-duty officer deaths reported by the National Law Enforcement Officer Memorial Fund, characterizations of the "Biden border crisis," and a statement that it is in the interest of law enforcement for Congress to enact border security legislation and for the President to utilize existing authorities, "including under section 212(f) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1182(f))." These findings are hortatory and impose no operative legal obligation; the reference to INA § 212(f) is descriptive and does not amend or invoke that authority.

Section 3 is the sole operative provision. It requires the Attorney General, "not later than 180 days after the date of enactment," to submit to Congress a report on the impact the border situation is having on law enforcement officers at all four governmental levels. The report must address seven enumerated matters: (1) the estimated dollar value of all resources devoted to addressing the border crisis and the extent to which those resources are diverted from law enforcement agencies; (2) officer exposure to fentanyl arising from encounters with "illegal aliens" at the border and within the United States, including the nationality of each such alien; (3) officer injuries connected to the border crisis or fentanyl exposure; (4) officer morale; (5) the effect on law enforcement recruiting and hiring; (6) estimated State expenditures on local law enforcement efforts to investigate, intercept, and process trafficked fentanyl, encompassing the entire evidence lifecycle from collection and analysis through storage and destruction; and (7) the number of officers reassigned and local resources reallocated for such fentanyl-related activities across the same evidence lifecycle.

The bill establishes no enforcement mechanism, funding, penalty, or ongoing reporting requirement beyond the single 180-day deliverable, and specifies no effective date other than that keyed to enactment.

The Swanson and Hugh Butler Reservoirs Land Conveyances Act (Public Law 118-185) directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner of Reclamation, to transfer certain federal land at Swanson Reservoir and Hugh Butler Reservoir in Nebraska to Hitchcock County and Frontier County.

The land involved consists of five parcels: permitted cabin lots and concession lands at each reservoir, plus concession land at Swanson, totaling roughly 77 acres. Within three years of enactment, the Secretary must make good-faith efforts to negotiate and enter into "title transfer agreements" with each county to convey all federal interest in the applicable parcels. The agreements must require that each parcel be conveyed in whole, not subdivided, and that the receiving county demonstrate the technical and financial capacity to operate and maintain the land and bring it into compliance with state fire, safety, and health codes within two years of conveyance.

As consideration, each county must pay the fair market value of the land, determined by a third-party appraisal conducted under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice. Permit-holder improvements are excluded from the appraised value, while anticipated future federal revenues (such as water service contracts and aid to irrigation) are included. Payments are made available to the Secretary, subject to appropriation, for operating the two reservoirs. Counties must also pay survey and administrative costs in advance.

Counties must manage the land for substantially its current uses or for recreation, public access, fish and wildlife habitat, or preservation of natural character. Reconveyance is generally prohibited, except at no cost to a Nebraska public or governmental entity meeting specified conditions.

Conveyances are subject to existing rights, reservoir operational requirements, flowage easements, mineral rights, existing permits, and deed restrictions barring new permanent structures below specified elevations. The United States is held harmless from various liabilities, and temporary flooding is not deemed a taking.

Existing management agreements remain in force until conveyance or three years after enactment. If no agreement is reached within three years, the Secretary continues managing the unaffected land under applicable law. Approved December 23, 2024.

Public Law 118-185, the "Swanson and Hugh Butler Reservoirs Land Conveyances Act" (H.R. 8413, enacted December 23, 2024), authorizes and directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner of Reclamation, to convey specified parcels of Federal land at Swanson Reservoir (Trenton Dam) and Hugh Butler Reservoir (Red Willow Dam)—both components of the Pick-Sloan Missouri Basin Program, Frenchman-Cambridge Division, authorized under section 9 of the Flood Control Act of 1944—to Hitchcock County and Frontier County, Nebraska.

Section 2 defines the five conveyable parcels (collectively "requested Federal land"): the Lakeview Lodge Permitted Concession Land, and the Red Willow and Swanson Permitted Cabin Land and Permitted Concession Land, delineated by referenced Bureau of Reclamation maps.

Section 3(a)(1) imposes a deadline of not later than three years after enactment for the Secretary to make good faith efforts to negotiate and enter into "title transfer agreements" conveying all requested United States right, title, and interest. Conveyance conditions include conveyance in whole, a prohibition on subdivision, and a demonstration plan addressing the county's technical/financial capacity and compliance with State fire, safety, and health codes within two years of conveyance. Section 3(a)(2) directs negotiation under the criteria of subtitle A of title VIII of the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act (43 U.S.C. 2901 et seq.), notwithstanding section 8002(3)(B) (43 U.S.C. 2902(3)(B)).

Section 3(a)(4) requires consideration equal to fair market value, determined by a Secretary-approved third-party appraiser under USPAP, excluding permit-holder improvements but accounting for foregone future federal revenue streams; disputes resolve under 43 C.F.R. § 2201.4. Payments are "available to the Secretary, subject to further appropriation," for reservoir operations—an authorization, not an appropriation. Counties bear all survey and administrative costs in advance. Section 3(a)(5) restricts post-conveyance use to substantially existing purposes or enumerated recreation/public-purpose, public-access, habitat, or preservation uses.

Section 3(b) bars subsequent reconveyance except at no cost to a Nebraska-recognized public/governmental entity meeting specified adverse-impact, management-capacity, and public-access conditions.

Section 4 subjects conveyances to valid existing rights, Pick-Sloan operational requirements, reserved flowage easements, management-agreement reservations, mineral rights and encumbrances of record as of enactment, elevation-based deed restrictions (2,785 feet at Swanson; 2,628 feet at Hugh Butler), and access easements. It disclaims United States liability for flood damage, requires county indemnification/hold-harmless, preserves Federal Tort Claims Act limits without expansion, and provides that temporary flooding is not a taking.

Section 5 continues the three management agreements and permits in force during the interim period ending the later of three years after enactment or the conveyance date; if no agreement is executed within three years, the Secretary manages the unconveyed land under applicable law.

expert.summary:
### Legislative Summary: Swanson and Hugh Butler Reservoirs Land Conveyances Act (P.L. 118-185)

#### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism
The primary purpose of the Act is to direct the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner of Reclamation, to convey all right, title, and interest of the United States in specified Federal lands and waters at Swanson Reservoir and Hugh Butler Reservoir to Hitchcock County and Frontier County, Nebraska. The operative mechanism is the execution of bilateral title transfer agreements that establish the legal, financial, and administrative terms of the conveyances.

#### Major Provisions and Statutory Authorities
*   **Negotiation and Execution of Title Transfer Agreements (Section 3(a)):** The Act imposes a statutory deadline of three years from the date of enactment (December 23, 2024) for the Secretary to make good faith efforts to negotiate and enter into title transfer agreements with Hitchcock and Frontier Counties. Section 3(a)(2) mandates that negotiations proceed under the criteria, terms, and conditions of subtitle A of title VIII of the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act (43 U.S.C. § 2901 et seq.), notwithstanding the exclusion in 43 U.S.C. § 2902(3)(B).
*   **Conveyance Conditions and Management Plans (Section 3(a)(1)):** As conditions precedent to conveyance, the agreements must prohibit subdivision of the parcels and require the counties to submit plans demonstrating:
    1.  Technical and financial capability to permanently operate and maintain the lands; and
    2.  Compliance with state fire, safety, and health codes within two years post-conveyance.
*   **Land Use Restrictions (Section 3(a)(5)):** Transferred lands must be managed for substantially the same purposes as of the date of enactment, or for recreation, public access, fish and wildlife habitat, or natural character preservation consistent with the Recreation and Public Purposes Act (43 U.S.C. § 869 et seq.).
*   **Reconveyance Limitations (Section 3(b)):** Subsequent reconveyance by the counties is generally prohibited. Section 3(b)(2) provides a narrow exception permitting reconveyance at no cost to a recognized Nebraska public or governmental entity (e.g., state agencies, natural resource districts, or irrigation/reclamation districts), provided the county demonstrates an impending adverse impact, the recipient has the capacity to maintain the historical management purposes, and public access is preserved.
*   **Reservations, Easements, and Deed Restrictions (Section 4(a)):** Conveyances are subject to valid existing rights, Pick-Sloan Missouri River Basin Program operational requirements, and federal flowage easements. The Act mandates deed restrictions prohibiting new permanent structures below 2,785 feet at Swanson Reservoir and 2,628 feet at Hugh Butler Reservoir. It also preserves existing mineral rights, permits, licenses, leases, and rights-of-way of record, and requires the granting of easements for vehicular access and existing permitted water-use improvements (e.g., docks and boathouses).
*   **Interim Management (Section 5):** During the transition period (ending on the later of three years post-enactment or the date of conveyance), existing management agreements and permits remain in effect. If a county fails to execute a title transfer agreement within the three-year deadline, the Secretary must resume management of the non-transferred lands under applicable federal law.

#### Financial Provisions and Funding Mechanics
*   **Consideration and Valuation (Section 3(a)(4)(A)):** The counties must pay fair market value for the lands, determined by a third-party appraiser approved by the Secretary. The appraisal must comply with the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, exclude permit-holder improvements, resolve disputes pursuant to 43 C.F.R. § 2201.4, and account for future federal income streams (e.g., water service, repayment contracts, and irrigation aid).
*   **Authorization of Appropriations:** Under Section 3(a)(4)(A)(iii), the acquisition revenues paid to the Secretary are made available for activities relating to the operation of the Hugh Butler and Swanson Reservoirs, subject to further appropriation (constituting an authorization rather than a direct appropriation).
*   **Administrative Costs (Section 3(a)(4)(B)):** The counties must pay all survey and administrative costs in advance of the conveyance.

#### Liability, Indemnification, and Sovereign Immunity (Section 4(b))
The Act immunizes the United States from liability for flood damage or third-party acts, except as provided under the Federal Tort Claims Act (28 U.S.C. § 2671 et seq.) for pre-enactment federal acts or omissions. The acquiring counties (and subsequent public transferees) must indemnify and hold the United States harmless against claims arising from reservoir operations, boundary surveys, or flood-related structural displacement. Temporary flooding of the properties is contractually and statutorily defined as not constituting a constitutional taking.

No new permanent buildings can be built below certain heights near the water—2,785 feet at Swanson and 2,628 feet at Hugh Butler. The counties agree not to blame the United States for flood damage. If no deal is reached in three years, the government will continue managing the land as before.

The Swanson and Hugh Butler Reservoirs Land Conveyances Act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner of Reclamation, to convey certain federal land at Swanson Reservoir and Hugh Butler Reservoir in Nebraska to Hitchcock County and Frontier County. The Act establishes a framework requiring the Secretary to make good faith efforts to negotiate and enter into title transfer agreements with each county within three years of enactment (December 23, 2024).

Section 2 defines key terms, including the five parcels constituting “requested Federal land”: Lakeview Lodge Permitted Concession Land, Red Willow Permitted Cabin Land, Red Willow Permitted Concession Land, Swanson Permitted Cabin Land, and Swanson Permitted Concession Land. The definitions cross-reference specific Bureau of Reclamation maps dated August 2023 and March 2024.

Section 3(a) prescribes the terms of conveyance. Title transfer agreements must provide for conveyance of the applicable parcel in whole, without subdivision, and include a plan demonstrating the county's technical and financial capability to permanently operate and maintain the land and to address state fire, safety, and health codes within two years post-conveyance. The Secretary must negotiate these agreements in accordance with subtitle A of title VIII of the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act (43 U.S.C. 2901 et seq.), notwithstanding 43 U.S.C. 2902(3)(B). Consideration is fair market value determined by a third-party appraisal conducted under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, excluding permit-holder improvements and accounting for future income streams from water service contracts, new contracts, irrigation aid, and other authorized sources. Appraisal disputes are resolved under 43 C.F.R. § 2201.4. Amounts paid are available to the Secretary, subject to further appropriation, for operations at the reservoirs. Conveyance costs are borne by the county in advance. Post-conveyance management must be for substantially the same purposes, or for recreation and public purposes consistent with the Recreation and Public Purposes Act (43 U.S.C. 869 et seq.), public access, fish and wildlife habitat, or preservation of natural character. Section 3(b) prohibits subsequent reconveyance except, under specified conditions, to certain publicly owned or governmental entities within the State, at no cost, and subject to continuing the same management purposes and public access.

Section 4 subjects conveyances to valid existing rights, Pick-Sloan Missouri River Basin Program operational requirements, flowage easements, reservations in the named management agreements, mineral rights and rights-of-way of record as of the date of enactment, deed restrictions prohibiting new permanent structures below specified elevations, and easements for access and improvements. The United States is not liable for flood damage or acts or omissions of permit holders or the counties, except for pre-enactment acts or omissions of the United States. The counties (and any subsequent governmental transferee) must indemnify and hold harmless the United States for claims arising from dam and reservoir operations, survey and conveyance processes, or flood-related damage. Temporary flooding or flood damage is not a taking, and nothing in the Act increases federal tort liability beyond chapter 171 of title 28.

Section 5 provides that the Lakeview Lodge, Red Willow, and Swanson Management Agreements and applicable permits remain in force and effect for the period beginning on enactment and ending on the later of three years post-enactment or the conveyance date. If a title transfer agreement is not entered into by the three-year deadline, the Secretary shall manage the unconveyed land according to applicable law.

# Summary of H.R. 8580 — Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2025

## Purpose
This bill provides federal funding for military construction, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and related agencies for fiscal year 2025 (ending September 30, 2025). It is an annual appropriations bill. The text shown passed the House on June 5, 2024, and was placed on the Senate calendar on September 12, 2024.

## Major Provisions

**Title I — Military Construction (Department of Defense):** Appropriates funds for construction and family housing across the Army, Navy/Marine Corps, Air Force, Defense-Wide activities, the National Guard, and Reserve components, plus the NATO Security Investment Program and the Base Closure Account. It includes additional amounts for laboratory facilities, child development centers, barracks, demolition, natural-disaster repairs, and unfunded-priority projects. Administrative provisions impose conditions such as American steel requirements, restrictions on foreign contractors, and congressional notification requirements.

**Title II — Department of Veterans Affairs:** Funds veterans benefits (compensation, pensions, readjustment, insurance, housing and other loan programs), the Veterans Health Administration (medical services, community care, support, facilities, and research), the National Cemetery Administration, departmental administration, information technology, the electronic health record system, the Office of Inspector General, construction, state facility/cemetery grants, and the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund. Many health accounts are funded as advance appropriations becoming available October 1, 2025. Provisions establish transfer authorities, reporting requirements, and policy conditions.

**Title III — Related Agencies:** Funds the American Battle Monuments Commission, U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, Arlington National Cemetery, and the Armed Forces Retirement Home.

**Title IV — General Provisions:** Establishes government-wide spending restrictions and policy riders.

## Notable Conditions and Riders
The bill prohibits funds for: gender-affirming surgical or hormone therapy; most abortions (with exceptions for rape, incest, or life endangerment); diversity, equity, and inclusion training; "Critical Race Theory"; enforcing certain COVID-19 vaccine and mask mandates; and implementing specified executive orders on climate and equity. It restricts purchases of computer equipment tied to China, conditions release of 25% of electronic-health-record funds on certifications, and limits actions affecting firearm background-check reporting and state marijuana program participation.

## Effective Dates
Funds generally cover fiscal year 2025; certain VA medical accounts become available October 1, 2025, and various construction funds remain available through September 30, 2029.

H.R. 8580, the "Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2025," is a regular appropriations bill making discretionary and mandatory appropriations for FY 2025 (fiscal year ending September 30, 2025) across four titles. It passed the House June 5, 2024, and was placed on the Senate calendar (PCS) September 12, 2024. The text contains numerous placeholder amendments (e.g., "(increased by $X)(reduced by $X)") reflecting floor-amendment artifacts that net to zero.

**Title I – Department of Defense (Military Construction).** Appropriates funds by component for acquisition and construction of military facilities as authorized by law, including Army ($2,217,757,000), Navy/Marine Corps ($4,332,414,000), Air Force ($3,268,276,000), and Defense-Wide ($3,500,083,000, with transfer authority), each available until September 30, 2029, with caps on planning/design funds subject to Secretarial override and congressional notification. Additional appropriations fund the National Guard and Reserve components (per chapter 1803, title 10), the NATO Security Investment Program (10 U.S.C. 2806), the DoD Base Closure Account (10 U.S.C. 2687 note), family housing accounts, and the Family Housing/Unaccompanied Housing Improvement Funds (10 U.S.C. 2883). Administrative provisions (Secs. 101–133) impose standard restrictions: cost-plus contract approval thresholds, American-steel and U.S.-contractor preferences, notification requirements, reprogramming per DoD FMR 7000.14-R, and prohibitions on funds for closure/realignment of Naval Station Guantanamo Bay (Sec. 133). Several additional appropriations (Secs. 124, 128–132) are conditioned on prior authorization and submission/approval of expenditure plans.

**Title II – Department of Veterans Affairs.** Provides current-year and advance (FY 2026) appropriations for mandatory benefit accounts (Compensation and Pensions; Readjustment Benefits; Insurance) and loan accounts, plus discretionary appropriations for VBA operations, VHA Medical Services ($75,039,000,000), Medical Community Care, Medical Support and Compliance, Medical Facilities, research, National Cemetery Administration, IT Systems, the Electronic Health Record system ($894,000,000, with 25% withheld until July 1, 2025 pending certifications), construction accounts, and the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund ($22,800,000,000). Administrative provisions (Secs. 201–261) grant conditional transfer authority (subject to congressional approval), and impose policy riders including prohibitions on abortion funding (Sec. 255, with rape/incest/life exceptions), gender-affirming surgical/hormone care (Sec. 256), phase-out of canine/feline/primate research by March 9, 2026 (Sec. 246), and SSN authentication discontinuance (Sec. 236, superseding P.L. 117-328 §237). Sec. 219 repeals section 220 of Title II of division A of P.L. 118-42.

**Title III – Related Agencies.** Funds the American Battle Monuments Commission, the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims ($47,200,000), Army cemeterial expenses (Arlington), and the Armed Forces Retirement Home.

**Title IV – General Provisions (Secs. 401–430).** Government-wide riders prohibit funds for implementing enumerated Executive Orders (Secs. 414, 419, 420), diversity/equity/inclusion activities (Sec. 417), "Critical Race Theory" (Sec. 415), Guantanamo detainee transfers (Sec. 412), and certain PRC-linked IT procurement (Sec. 421). Sec. 401 restricts availability to the current fiscal year absent express provision.

### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism

H.R. 8580, the **Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2025**, is an appropriations act that provides fiscal year (FY) 2025 discretionary appropriations, advance appropriations for FY 2026, and designated multi-year or indefinite funds. Its primary purpose is to fund military construction, family housing, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and specified related agencies. The operative mechanism is the direct statutory allocation of Treasury funds to designated accounts, subject to specified transfer authorities, reprogramming limitations, conditions precedent, and restrictive riders.

---

### Major Provisions by Title

#### Title I: Department of Defense (DoD)
*   **Military Construction Appropriations:** Allocates FY 2025 funds, remaining available until September 30, 2029, for the acquisition, construction, and installation of public works, installations, and facilities for the Army ($2,217,757,000), Navy and Marine Corps ($4,332,414,000), Air Force ($3,268,276,000), Defense-Wide ($3,500,083,000), and reserve components pursuant to 10 U.S.C. chapter 1803.
*   **Planning and Design Caps:** Imposes statutory ceilings on planning, design, and architect-engineer services within each military department's construction account (e.g., $334,738,000 for the Army), unless the respective Secretary determines additional obligations are necessary and notifies the congressional appropriations committees.
*   **NATO Security Investment Program:** Appropriates $433,864,000, to remain available until expended, for collective defense construction under 10 U.S.C. § 2806.
*   **Base Closure Account:** Appropriates $547,961,000, to remain available until expended, to the DoD Base Closure Account established under section 2906(a) of the Defense Base Closure and Realignment Act of 1990 (10 U.S.C. § 2687 note).
*   **Family Housing:** Appropriates funds for family housing construction and operation and maintenance (O&M) for the Army, Navy/Marine Corps, Air Force, and Defense-Wide. Under Section 119, O&M family housing accounts serve as the exclusive funding source for general or flag officer quarters, capping annual maintenance at $20,000 per unit absent prior congressional notification.
*   **Housing Improvement Funds:** Appropriates $8,195,000 to the Family Housing Improvement Fund and $497,000 to the Military Unaccompanied Housing Improvement Fund, to remain available until expended, for initiatives under 10 U.S.C. § 2883.
*   **Administrative Provisions:**
    *   **Sec. 111 & 112 (Procurement Restrictions):** Restricts architect-engineer contracts exceeding $500,000 in Japan, NATO countries, or Arabian Gulf border countries to U.S. firms or joint ventures. Restricts Pacific territory and Arabian Gulf military construction contracts exceeding $1,000,000 to domestic contractors, subject to a 20 percent price-differential exception or Marshallese contractor exception on Kwajalein Atoll.
    *   **Sec. 117 (Transfer Authority):** Authorizes the transfer of funds from "Family Housing" and "Military Construction" accounts to the Family Housing Improvement Fund and the Military Unaccompanied Housing Improvement Fund, respectively, subject to a 30-day prior notification period (or 14 days for electronic notifications under 10 U.S.C. §§ 480 and 2883).
    *   **Sec. 124 (Unfunded Priorities):** Appropriates additional construction funds (e.g., $167,000,000 for the Army) restricted to projects on FY 2025 unfunded priority lists, subject to prior authorization and a 60-day post-enactment expenditure plan submission.

#### Title II: Department of Veterans Affairs (VA)
*   **Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA):**
    *   **Compensation and Pensions:** Appropriates $9,820,699,000 for FY 2025 (in addition to advance appropriations), and $204,481,753,000 as an advance appropriation for FY 2026, to remain available until expended, for benefits under chapters 11, 13, 15, 18, 23, 51, 53, 55, and 61 of Title 38.
    *   **Readjustment Benefits:** Appropriates $2,657,656,000 for FY 2025 and $17,614,235,000 as an advance appropriation for FY 2026, to remain available until expended, for chapters 21, 30–36, 39, 41, 51, 53, 55, and 61 of Title 38.
*   **Veterans Health Administration (VHA):**
    *   **Medical Services:** Appropriates $75,039,000,000 as an advance appropriation for FY 2026, to remain available until September 30, 2026, with $2,000,000,000 remaining available until September 30, 2027.
    *   **Medical Community Care:** Appropriates $34,000,000,000 as an advance appropriation for FY 2026, to remain available until September 30, 2026, with $2,000,000,000 remaining available until September 30, 2027.
    *   **Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund:** Appropriates $22,800,000,000 as an advance appropriation for FY 2026, to remain available until expended, for environmental hazard exposure health care and benefits under 38 U.S.C. § 324.
*   **Departmental Administration:**
    *   **Information Technology Systems:** Appropriates $6,231,680,000, segmenting allocations for pay ($1,686,245,270), operations and maintenance ($4,544,475,000), and development ($960,000).
    *   **Veterans Electronic Health Record:** Appropriates $894,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2026. Under a condition precedent, 25 percent of these funds are withheld until July 1, 2025, contingent upon the Secretary submitting a system stability report and written certifications regarding deployment readiness.
    *   **Construction, Major Projects:** Appropriates $2,069,000,000 for projects exceeding the threshold in 38 U.S.C. § 8104(a)(3)(A), with $1,265,000,000 remaining available until September 30, 2029, and $803,700,000 remaining available until expended.
*   **Administrative Provisions:**
    *   **Sec. 201 & 202 (Transfer Authorities):** Permits transfers between VBA entitlement accounts (subject to a 30-day congressional review or prior approval) and VHA medical accounts (subject to a 1 percent cap for notification-only transfers, and prior approval for transfers exceeding 1 percent or involving "Medical Facilities").
    *   **Sec. 218 (IT Transfers):** Authorizes transfers from VHA, VBA, and departmental administration accounts to "Information Technology Systems," capped at a 10 percent aggregate increase of the IT account and subject to prior congressional approval.
    *   **Sec. 219 & 220 (Joint Facility Transfers):** Authorizes transfers of up to $594,828,000 (FY 2025) and $664,625,000 (FY 2026) to the Joint DoD-VA Medical Facility Demonstration Fund established under section 1704 of Public Law 111-84. Repeals section 220 of division A of Public Law 118-42.
    *   **Sec. 233 (Fertility and Adoption Benefits):** Authorizes the use of "Medical Services" funds for fertility counseling, assisted reproductive technology (as defined in the April 3, 2012, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Health Affairs memorandum, excluding duration limits on embryo cryopreservation), and adoption reimbursement for covered veterans with service-connected infertility.
    *   **Sec. 236 (SSN De-identification):** Mandates that the VA discontinue using Social Security numbers to authenticate individuals in its information systems, superseding section 237 of division J of Public Law 117-328.

The bill operates by making specified sums available from the Treasury, subject to terms, conditions, and transfer authorities.

**Title I — Department of Defense.** Appropriates funds for military construction for the Army, Navy and Marine Corps, Air Force, Defense-Wide, Army and Air National Guard, and the reserve components, generally to remain available until September 30, 2029. Each account caps amounts for study, planning, design, and architect-engineer services and permits exceeding those caps only with committee notification. The Department of Defense Base Closure Account receives $547,961,000 (available until expended). Family housing construction and operation accounts are appropriated, with availability periods as specified.

Administrative provisions (Sections 101–133) impose numerous restrictions and authorities: e.g., prohibition on cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts over $25,000 without Secretarial approval (Sec. 101); advance of funds to FHWA for access roads (Sec. 103); limitations on land purchases exceeding appraised value (Sec. 105); prohibitions on new bases without specific appropriation (Sec. 104), on transfer of activities under minor construction (Sec. 107), and on procurement of steel where U.S. producers were denied competition (Sec. 108). Section 117 authorizes transfers to Family Housing and Unaccompanied Housing Improvement Funds subject to 30‑day (or 14‑day electronic) notification. Section 121 permits transfers of expired unobligated balances to “Foreign Currency Fluctuations, Construction, Defense.” Section 124 provides additional amounts across accounts ($357 million total) for projects on the military departments’ unfunded priority lists, conditioned on prior authorization and an expenditure plan within 60 days. Sections 128–132 appropriate additional sums for laboratory facilities, child development centers, barracks, and demolition, each conditioned on submission (and in some cases prior approval) of expenditure plans. Section 133 prohibits use of funds to close or realign Naval Station Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.

**Title II — Department of Veterans Affairs.** Makes appropriations for the Veterans Benefits Administration (Compensation and Pensions; Readjustment Benefits; Veterans Insurance and Indemnities; Housing Benefit Program Fund; Vocational Rehabilitation Loans; Native American Veteran Housing Loan Program; General Operating Expenses). The Compensation and Pensions account provides $9.82 billion (fiscal year 2025 advance) and $204.48 billion (to become available October 1, 2025). Readjustment Benefits and Insurance accounts similarly include advance appropriations for fiscal year 2026. The Veterans Health Administration receives appropriations for Medical Services ($75.039 billion, available October 1, 2025), Medical Community Care ($34 billion), Medical Support and Compliance ($12.7 billion), Medical Facilities ($9.7 billion), and Medical and Prosthetic Research ($923.5 million), with specified periods of availability and portions for longer-term obligations. The Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund receives $22.8 billion, available October 1, 2025, until expended. Construction accounts include Major Projects ($2.069 billion, with specific obligation deadlines) and Minor Projects ($380.5 million). Section 235 exempts certain tribally-owned contractors from Section 842 of Public Law 109‑115. Section 236 requires discontinuation of Social Security numbers for authentication. Section 242 provides Inspector General access rights and reporting. Section 246 restricts canine, feline, and non-human primate research, requiring Secretarial certification and a plan to end such research by March 9, 2026. anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.label: anthropic/claude-opus-4.8
anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The DETECT Fentanyl and Xylazine Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-186) directs the Science and Technology Directorate of the Department of Homeland Security to develop improved capabilities for detecting and identifying illicit drugs, including those present in very low concentrations, such as fentanyl and xylazine.

The bill amends Section 302 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 by adding a new responsibility. In coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), the Directorate must conduct research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analyses to improve the safety, effectiveness, and efficiency of detection equipment and the reference libraries used by federal, state, local, Tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies. This work specifically includes developing: (1) portable equipment capable of detecting and identifying drugs with minimal or no handling of the sample; (2) equipment that can separate complex mixtures containing low drug concentrations and high concentrations of cutting agents to enable field identification; and (3) technologies using machine learning or artificial intelligence (as defined in the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020) to predict whether substances in a sample are controlled substance analogues or new psychoactive substances not yet listed in existing reference libraries.

In carrying out these activities, the Under Secretary for Science and Technology must follow the recommendations and best practices in the National Institute of Standards and Technology's Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1) or any successor document. The Under Secretary must also set the Directorate's research and evaluation priorities based on the latest available information, including drugs identified as threats in the most recent Homeland Threat Assessment, the DEA's State and Territory Report on Enduring and Emerging Threats, or successor documents.

The Act includes a rule of construction stating that nothing in it limits the authority of agencies already managing or involved in drug equipment and reference libraries. The law was approved on December 23, 2024.
