expert.summary:
Public Law 118-186, the "Detection Equipment and Technology Evaluation to Counter the Threat of Fentanyl and Xylazine Act of 2024" (or "DETECT Fentanyl and Xylazine Act of 2024"), enacted December 23, 2024 (originating as H.R. 8663), directs the Department of Homeland Security's Science and Technology Directorate to develop enhanced capacity to detect and identify illicit substances present in very low concentrations. Its operative mechanism is an amendment to the enumerated responsibilities of the Under Secretary for Science and Technology under the Homeland Security Act of 2002.

Section 2 amends Section 302 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 182) by making conforming punctuation changes to paragraphs (13) and (14) and adding a new paragraph (15). New paragraph (15) authorizes the Directorate, in coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration, to carry out research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analyses to improve the safety, effectiveness, and efficiency of equipment and reference libraries used by Federal, State, local, Tribal, and territorial law enforcement for accurate drug detection. It enumerates three focus areas: (A) portable equipment capable of detecting and identifying drugs with minimal or no sample handling; (B) equipment able to separate complex mixtures containing low drug concentrations and high concentrations of cutting agents to enable signature extraction for field identification; and (C) technologies employing machine learning or artificial intelligence (as defined in Section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020, 15 U.S.C. 9401) and other techniques to predict whether sample substances are controlled substance analogues or new psychoactive substances not yet in available reference libraries.

Section 3 (codified as a note to 6 U.S.C. 182) imposes two requirements on the Under Secretary in carrying out the new Section 302(15): (1) adherence to the recommendations, guidelines, and best practices of the NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1) or any successor document; and (2) establishment of research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analysis priorities based on the latest available information, including specific drugs identified as threats in the latest DHS Homeland Threat Assessment, the latest DEA State and Territory Report on Enduring and Emerging Threats, or successor documents.

Section 4 (also codified as a 6 U.S.C. 182 note) is a rule of construction providing that nothing in the Act may be construed to limit the authority of agencies currently managing, overseeing, or otherwise involved in drug equipment and reference libraries.

The Act contains no appropriation and no separate authorization of appropriations; it confers authority and imposes procedural requirements without providing funding. It specifies no delayed effective date or sunset provision.

This bill, the "Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2025" (H.R. 8752), provides funding for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025. It passed the House of Representatives on June 28, 2024.

**Appropriations by area.** The bill funds DHS operations across five titles:
- **Departmental management and oversight** (Title I), including the Office of the Secretary, the Management Directorate, intelligence and situational awareness, and the Inspector General.
- **Security, enforcement, and investigations** (Title II), funding Customs and Border Protection (CBP, roughly $16.6 billion in operations), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE, roughly $10.5 billion), the Transportation Security Administration, the Coast Guard, and the Secret Service.
- **Protection and preparedness** (Title III), funding the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, FEMA grants, the Disaster Relief Fund ($22.7 billion), and the National Flood Insurance Fund.
- **Research, training, and services** (Title IV), funding citizenship services (E-Verify), training centers, the Science and Technology Directorate, and weapons-of-mass-destruction programs.

**Major policy provisions.** The bill sets specific conditions on spending, including:
- Requiring ICE to maintain at least 50,000 detention beds and enroll non-detained aliens in GPS monitoring.
- Allocating $600 million for border physical barriers (steel bollard barriers 18–30 feet high) and prohibiting funds to dismantle existing barriers.
- Prohibiting use of the CBP One app to facilitate parole, barring new border-crossing fees, and blocking certain enforcement-priority memos and asylum rules.
- Restricting funds for gender-affirming care in ICE custody and most ICE-funded abortions (with exceptions for rape, incest, or life endangerment).
- Prohibiting funding for diversity/equity executive orders, certain climate executive orders, a "Disinformation Governance Board," and electric-vehicle purchases.
- Reducing one named employee's salary to $1 and barring funding for Secretary Mayorkas's salary.
- Requiring extensive reporting, reprogramming notifications, and oversight access for Members of Congress to detention facilities.

**Rescissions.** The bill rescinds $600 million in prior border-barrier construction funds and $154 million from the Nonrecurring Expenses Fund.

Various provisions carry specific effective dates (e.g., contraceptive coverage provisions effective 30 and 180 days after enactment) and deadlines for reports and expenditure plans.

H.R. 8752, the "Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2025," is a regular annual appropriations bill providing discretionary funding for DHS for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025. As engrossed in the House, the bill's text reflects numerous parenthetical floor amendments (increases/reductions to account totals). It is organized in five titles and appropriates funds by account (Operations and Support; Procurement, Construction, and Improvements (PC&I); Research and Development; Federal Assistance), with account-specific availability periods and provisos.

**Title I (Departmental Management)** funds the Office of the Secretary, Management Directorate, Office of Intelligence and Analysis, and OIG. Administrative provisions impose reporting requirements (e.g., Sec. 101–102 IG and CFO reports), condition Treasury Forfeiture Fund transfers under 31 U.S.C. 9705(g)(4)(B) on prior notification (Sec. 103), and require quarterly acquisition-program briefings on Level 1/Level 2 programs (Sec. 105). Sec. 106 prohibits obligation for new pilots/demonstrations (defined as >10 FTE or ≥$5,000,000) absent documented objectives and reporting.

**Title II (Security, Enforcement, Investigations)** funds CBP, ICE, TSA, Coast Guard, and Secret Service. Notable directives: ICE funding must maintain not less than 50,000 detention beds and prioritize full-capacity detention with mandatory GPS Alternatives to Detention (Sec. 228); Sec. 211 allocates CBP PC&I funds, mandating steel bollard barriers 18–30 feet high per the August 1, 2020 Border Security Improvement Plan, with obligation beginning within 120 days. Numerous limitation riders defund specified policies: CBP One parole use (Sec. 213), the "Emergency Driving" directive (Sec. 214), the September 30, 2021 enforcement-priorities memorandum (Sec. 224), gender-affirming care (Sec. 227), and border-crossing fees (Sec. 207). Secs. 250–251 (effective 30 and 180 days after enactment, respectively) prohibit TRICARE cost-sharing for contraceptives and authorize 365-day contraceptive supply for Coast Guard beneficiaries under 10 U.S.C. 1074g/1075/1075a.

**Title III (Preparedness/Response)** funds CISA, FEMA, the Disaster Relief Fund ($22,741,000,000, designated under BBEDCA §251(b)(2)(D)), the National Flood Insurance Fund, and enumerated FEMA grant programs under the Homeland Security Act (6 U.S.C. 604–609a) and other statutes.

**Title IV** funds USCIS (E-Verify), FLETC, S&T, and CWMD. Sec. 406 authorizes an H-2B numerical-cap increase above INA §214(g)(1)(B).

**Title V (General Provisions)** sets reprogramming/transfer thresholds (Sec. 503; 5% transfer, 10% augmentation ceilings, June 15 cutoff). It rescinds $600,000,000 in prior-year CBP barrier funds (Public Law 116-260) (Sec. 550) and $154,000,000 from the Nonrecurring Expenses Fund (Sec. 551). Additional riders defund the "Circumvention of Lawful Pathways" and "Public Charge" rules, the Disinformation Governance Board, DHS equity/environmental-justice initiatives and enumerated Executive Orders, reduce a named employee's salary to $1 (Sec. 563), and prohibit funding Secretary Mayorkas's salary (Sec. 564).

This measure constitutes budget authority, not permanent authorizing law; provisions apply for fiscal year 2025 unless otherwise specified.

H.R. 8752, the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2025, is an appropriations act that provides fiscal year (FY) 2025 discretionary appropriations, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and its constituent agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025. The bill operates through five titles containing specific line-item appropriations, funding limitations, reporting mandates, and administrative provisions.

---

### Major Provisions by Title

#### Title I: Departmental Management, Intelligence, Situational Awareness, and Oversight
*   **Office of the Secretary and Executive Management:** Appropriates $281,358,000 (subject to specified legislative reductions and increases) for Operations and Support, with $22,151,000 available through September 30, 2026. It imposes a condition precedent withholding $5,000,000 from obligation until the Secretary submits responses to all questions for the record from FY 2026 budget hearings held prior to July 1.
*   **Management Directorate:** Appropriates $1,637,290,000 (subject to specified legislative reductions) for Operations and Support, and $54,337,000 (subject to specified legislative adjustments) for Procurement, Construction, and Improvements, available until September 30, 2027. It authorizes the Federal Protective Service to use credited security fee collections without fiscal year limitation.
*   **Intelligence, Analysis, and Situational Awareness:** Appropriates $345,360,000 for Operations and Support, with $105,701,000 available through September 30, 2026.
*   **Office of Inspector General (OIG):** Appropriates $225,294,000 for Operations and Support, authorizing up to $300,000 for confidential operational expenses.
*   **Administrative Provisions:** 
    *   **Sec. 101:** Mandates that the Secretary report non-competitive grants and contracts from FY 2024–2025 to the OIG by October 15, 2025, and requires the OIG to submit a compliance assessment to the congressional appropriations committees by February 15, 2026.
    *   **Sec. 102:** Requires monthly budget and staffing reports from the Chief Financial Officer (CFO) within 30 days of each month's end.
    *   **Sec. 103:** Conditions the obligation of Treasury Forfeiture Fund transfers under 31 U.S.C. § 9705(g)(4)(B) on prior notification to the appropriations committees.
    *   **Sec. 105:** Requires quarterly briefings by the Under Secretary for Management on Level 1 and Level 2 acquisition programs and the submission of approved Acquisition Decision Memorandums within five business days of approval.
    *   **Sec. 106:** Prohibits the obligation of funds for new pilots or demonstrations (defined as experiments utilizing more than 10 full-time equivalents or costing $5,000,000 or more) unless documented objectives, assessment methodologies, and implementation plans are established and, for Operations and Support funds, reported to the appropriations committees.

#### Title II: Security, Enforcement, and Investigations
*   **U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP):**
    *   **Operations and Support:** Appropriates $16,566,247,000 (subject to specified legislative adjustments), with $550,000,000 available through September 30, 2026.     *   **Operations and Support:** Appropriates $10,817,225,000 (subject to specified legislative adjustments), with $300,000,000 available through September 30, 2026. Security service fees under 49 U.S.C. § 44940 are credited as offsetting collections, reducing the general fund contribution dollar-for-dollar to an estimated maximum of $7,957,225,000.
    *   **Procurement, Construction, and Improvements:** Appropriates $198,428,000 (subject to specified legislative adjustments), available through September 30, 2027.

*   **Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA):** Appropriates $2,437,285,000 for Operations and Support (with $23,698,000 available through September 30, 2026) and $493,572,000 for Procurement, Construction, and Improvements (available through September 30, 2027). *   **Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA):**

    *   **National Flood Insurance Fund:** Appropriates $239,785,000, available through September 30, 2026, derived from offsetting collections under 42 U.S.C. § 4015(d).

The bill is organized in five titles, each addressing a functional grouping of DHS components, and includes numerous administrative provisions, general provisions, and rescissions.

**Title I** appropriates funds for Departmental Management, Intelligence, Situational Awareness, and Oversight, including the Office of the Secretary and Executive Management, the Management Directorate, the Office of Intelligence and Analysis, and the Office of Inspector General. Section 101 requires the Secretary to report all non-competitive grants and contracts from FY2024–2025 to the Inspector General by October 15, 2025, with IG review due to the Appropriations Committees by February 15, 2026. Section 102 mandates monthly budget and staffing reports from the Chief Financial Officer. Section 103 conditions transfers from the Treasury Forfeiture Fund (31 U.S.C. 9705(g)(4)(B)) on prior notification to the Appropriations Committees. Sections 105 and 106 impose quarterly acquisition briefing requirements and pilot program documentation and reporting obligations, respectively.

**Title II** appropriates funds for U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the Coast Guard, and the U.S. Secret Service. Section 211 earmarks $1,390,338,000 for CBP procurement with specified allocations including $600,000,000 for physical barriers, requiring steel bollard pedestrian barriers of 18–30 feet effective height with anti-climb and anti-dig features at locations identified in the August 1, 2020 Border Security Improvement Plan, with obligation required within 120 days of enactment. Section 212 prohibits dismantling existing U.S.–Mexico barriers unless simultaneously repaired or replaced. Section 213 bars use of the CBP One application to facilitate parole. Sections 218–219 address section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1357(g)) delegations, prohibiting reduction in participation except where the IG determines material breach. Section 220 bars continuation of detention contracts with facilities receiving two consecutive sub-adequate performance evaluations. Section 228 requires ICE to maintain detention at full facility capacity and mandate GPS monitoring for all non-detained docket aliens. Sections 225, 226, 227, 230, 231, and 232 impose restrictions on interior transport, abortion funding, gender-affirming care, alien identification cards, Alternatives to Detention standards, and protected-area enforcement guidelines, respectively. Sections 250–251 prohibit TRICARE cost-sharing for contraceptives for Coast Guard members and dependents, effective 30 and 180 days post-enactment, respectively.

**Title III** appropriates funds for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and the National Flood Insurance Fund. Section 302 raises the administrative cost cap to 5 percent for specified grant programs. Section 304 imposes a $1,000,000 rescission penalty for premature public grant announcements. The Disaster Relief Fund receives $22,741,000,000, designated as disaster relief under section 251(b)(2)(D) of the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985.

**Title IV** appropriates funds for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers, the Science and Technology Directorate, and the Countering Weapons of Mass Destruction Office. Section 406 authorizes the Secretary to increase H-2B visa numbers above the statutory cap (8 U.S.C. 1184(g)(1)(B)) by the highest returning-worker participation level. Section 408 bars H-1B petition approval for entities identified under section 1260H of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for FY2021.

**Title V** contains general provisions. Section 503 establishes reprogramming and transfer notification requirements with specified thresholds and a June 15 cutoff. Section 507 mandates advance notification for grants, contracts, and awards exceeding specified amounts. Section 527 guarantees Members of Congress and designated employees access to DHS detention facilities without prior notice. Section 528 restricts restraints on pregnant detainees. Sections 536 and 537 prohibit funding to entities identified under section 1260H and transfer of Guantanamo detainees, respectively. Section 538 requires bimonthly southwest border arrival estimates, with suspension of reprogramming authority for noncompliance. Sections 543–567 impose numerous policy riders, including prohibitions on the Circumvention of Lawful Pathways rule, Disinformation Governance Board, classification of speech as mis- or disinformation, implementation of specified Executive Orders, the Public Charge rule, electric vehicle purchases, COVID-19 mask mandates, environmental justice strategies, Safe Mobility Offices, and the salary of the Secretary of Homeland Security. Sections 550–551 rescind $600,000,000 from CBP barrier construction balances (Public Law 116-260) and $154,000,000 from the DHS Nonrecurring Expenses Fund. Section 553 prohibits reduction of operating hours at 15 specified northern border ports of entry.

**Major Appropriations.** The bill funds the House of Representatives (approximately $1.93 billion for salaries and expenses, including Members' representational allowances, committees, and intern compensation), the Capitol Police (over $830 million), the Architect of the Capitol (covering the Capitol building, grounds, office buildings, and power plant), the Library of Congress (including the Copyright Office and Congressional Research Service), the Government Publishing Office, the Government Accountability Office (about $896.7 million), the Congressional Budget Office, and several smaller offices and joint committees. It also provides $174,000 to the widow of the late Representative Donald M. Payne, Jr.

**Notable Provisions and Changes to Existing Law:**
- Unspent Members' representational allowances must be returned to the Treasury for deficit or debt reduction (Sec. 110).
- Vehicle leasing from Member allowances is capped at $1,000 per month per vehicle (Sec. 111).
- Capitol Police training outside the U.S. requires prior approval from the Capitol Police Board (Sec. 115).
- Funds may not be used to purchase drones made in or affiliated with the People's Republic of China, except for national security.
- The bill amends laws on Energy Policy Act lease requirements (Sec. 113), the child care center fund (Sec. 114), and fiduciary relationships for Members providing medical or dental care (Sec. 211).
- Section 209 prohibits procurement of certain telecommunications and surveillance equipment from named Chinese companies and foreign adversaries, with phased effective dates and a limited waiver authority.
- Section 212 bars funding for diversity, equity, and inclusion training promoting specified "divisive concepts" related to race or sex.
- Section 213 prohibits discriminatory action against persons holding the belief that marriage is between one man and one woman.
- Section 214 blocks cost-of-living pay adjustments for Members of Congress in fiscal year 2025.

The bill includes general provisions on transfers, consulting contracts, Capitol tours, and computer network content. It was reported by the House Committee on Appropriations on June 17, 2024.

Sec. 115 amends 5 U.S.C. 4120 to require Capitol Police Board approval for international training. Sec. 117 grants the Architect cooperative-agreement and plant-exchange authority.

### Precise Technical Summary of H.R. 8772

H.R. 8772, the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 2025, is a first-session, 118th Congress bill that provides discretionary appropriations for the legislative branch of the United States Government for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025. The bill’s primary purpose is to fund the operations, salaries, and capital expenses of the House of Representatives, joint congressional offices, and legislative branch support agencies.

#### Title I: Legislative Branch Appropriations and Mandates

Title I provides line-item appropriations and establishes specific statutory conditions, including:

*   **House of Representatives:** Appropriates $1,932,655,000 for salaries and expenses. This includes $843,605,000 for Members’ Representational Allowances (MRAs) and specific allocations for intern compensation under 2 U.S.C. § 5322a, 2 U.S.C. § 5106, and Public Law 117-103, capping individual Member office intern expenditures at $46,800 for legislative year 2025.
*   **Administrative Provisions (House):** 
    *   **Section 110:** Restricts FY 2025 MRA funds to FY 2025 availability and mandates that unexpended balances be deposited into the Treasury for deficit reduction or federal debt retirement.
    *   **Section 111:** Restricts the Chief Administrative Officer from making MRA payments for vehicle leases (excluding mobile district offices) exceeding $1,000 per month per vehicle.
    *   **Section 112:** Mandates that any federal entity assisting the House with cybersecurity must implement minimization procedures to preserve constitutional separation of powers and protect privileged legislative information.
    *   **Section 113:** Amends Section 303(f) of the Energy Policy Act of 1992 (42 U.S.C. § 13212(f)) to strike the House of Representatives from certain alternative fueled vehicle acquisition requirements, effective FY 2025 and thereafter.
    *   **Section 114:** Amends Section 312(d)(3) of the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 1992 (2 U.S.C. § 2062(d)(3)) to authorize the House Child Care Center Revolving Fund to pay for telecommunications expenses, effective FY 2025 and thereafter.
*   **Joint Items and Support Agencies:** Appropriates funds for the Joint Economic Committee ($4,283,000), Joint Committee on Taxation ($14,450,000), Office of the Attending Physician ($4,416,000), and Office of Congressional Accessibility Services ($1,814,000).
*   **Capitol Police:** Appropriates $619,257,000 for salaries (capping overtime at $74,976,000 absent Appropriations Committee notification) and $213,158,000 for general expenses. It bars the procurement of unmanned aircraft systems (drones) manufactured in or by entities affiliated with the People's Republic of China (PRC), except for national security purposes.
    *   **Section 115:** Amends 5 U.S.C. § 4120 to require prior approval from the Capitol Police Board for international employee training, effective FY 2025 and thereafter.
*   **Office of Congressional Workplace Rights & Congressional Budget Office:** Appropriates $8,150,000 and $73,259,000, respectively, earmarking at least $500,000 of CBO funds for transparency and modeling enhancements.
*   **Architect of the Capitol (AOC):** Appropriates funds across multiple accounts, including Capital Construction and Operations ($165,000,000) and House Office Buildings ($148,000,000).
    *   **Section 116:** Prohibits the AOC from paying contractor incentive or award fees for projects behind schedule or over budget, unless deviations are due to unforeseeable events or government-driven scope changes.
    *   **Section 117:** Authorizes the AOC, subject to committee approval, to enter into cooperative agreements and engage in plant material exchanges to support the Capitol Grounds and Arboretum, effective FY 2025 and thereafter.
*   **Library of Congress (LOC):** Appropriates $617,000,000 for salaries and expenses, $105,642,000 for the Copyright Office, $141,487,000 for the Congressional Research Service, and $65,205,000 for the National Library Service for the Blind and Print Disabled.
    *   **Section 118:** Establishes an FY 2025 obligational limit of $328,789,000 for the LOC’s non-appropriated reimbursable and revolving fund activities.
*   **Government Publishing Office (GPO):** Appropriates $83,000,000 for Congressional Publishing, subject to a 27-month printing limitation under 44 U.S.C. § 718.
*   **Government Accountability Office (GAO):** Appropriates $896,700,000, plus $33,424,000 in offsetting collections.

#### Title II: General Provisions

Title II establishes government-wide legislative branch restrictions and statutory amendments:

*   **Sections 201–206:** Prohibits the use of funds for private vehicle maintenance (Sec. 201); limits fund availability to FY 2025 unless expressly provided (Sec. 202); establishes rates of compensation as permanent law (Sec. 203); restricts consulting service contracts to public records (Sec. 204); limits the Legislative Branch Financial Managers Council shared costs to $2,000 (Sec. 205); and prohibits unauthorized interagency transfers (Sec. 206).
*   **Section 207:** Prohibits the AOC from restricting member- or staff-led guided tours of the Capitol, except under 2 U.S.C. § 2242(b)(8) or via Capitol Police Board security directives.
*   **Section 208:** Restricts computer networks established with these funds from accessing pornography, excepting law enforcement or official investigative activities.
*   **Section 209:** Prohibits the procurement of telecommunications or video surveillance equipment or services from Huawei Technologies Company, ZTE Corporation, Hytera Communications Corporation, Hangzhou Hikvision Digital Technology Company, Dahua Technology Company, or any entity connected to a "foreign adversary country" as defined in 10 U.S.C. § 4872(d). It provides a one-time, maximum two-year waiver mechanism subject to a supply-chain laydown and phase-out plan.
*   **Section 210:** Exempts the Director of the GPO and the Librarian of Congress from statutory pay-freeze limitations, effective calendar year 2025 and thereafter.
*   **Section 211:** Amends 5 U.S.C. § 13144 to clarify that direct patient care (medical or dental) provided by a Member of Congress does not constitute a "fiduciary relationship" for purposes of outside compensation limitations, effective FY 2025 and thereafter.
*   **Section 212:** Prohibits funding for diversity, equity, and inclusion training or implementation that promotes divisive concepts related to race or sex.
*   **Section 213:** Prohibits discriminatory actions by the Federal Government—including tax status alterations, deduction disallowances, or withholding of grants, contracts, and benefits—against any person based on a sincerely held religious belief or moral conviction that marriage is a union of one man and one woman.
*   **Section 214:** Bars any cost-of-living adjustment for Members of Congress under 2 U.S.C. § 4501 during FY 2025.

The FAFSA Deadline Act (Public Law 118-145) amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 to require that the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) be made available earlier in the application cycle.

Under prior law, Section 483(d)(4) of the Higher Education Act directed the Secretary of Education to make the FAFSA available no later than January 1 of the applicant's planned year of enrollment, and "to the maximum extent practicable," on or around October 1 of the year before enrollment. The Act replaces this language with a firm requirement that the application be made available no later than October 1 prior to the applicant's planned year of enrollment.

The Act also adds new certification and testimony requirements tied to each application processing cycle. Before each cycle begins, the Secretary must, no later than September 1, certify to the authorizing committees of Congress either that the Department of Education will meet the October 1 deadline, or that it will not meet that deadline. If the Secretary certifies that the deadline will not be met, the Secretary must, no later than September 30, testify before the authorizing committees regarding the anticipated failure to meet the deadline and the financial impact that failure will have on students and families.

The Act was approved on December 11, 2024.

The FAFSA Deadline Act (Pub. L. 118-145, enacted December 11, 2024, originating as H.R. 8932) amends Section 483(d)(4) of the Higher Education Act of 1965 (20 U.S.C. 1090(d)(4)) to establish an earlier, fixed availability deadline for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) processing cycle and to impose associated congressional certification and testimony obligations on the Secretary of Education.

Section 2 replaces the prior formulation—which required the FAFSA to be available "not later than January 1 of the applicant's planned year of enrollment," with a subsidiary aspiration to make it available "to the maximum extent practicable, on or around October 1"—with a single hard deadline: "not later than October 1 prior to the applicant's planned year of enrollment." This converts the former precatory October 1 target into a binding statutory deadline and eliminates the January 1 backstop.

Section 3 further amends Section 483(d)(4) by restructuring the existing text as subparagraph (A) ("In general") and adding a new subparagraph (B) ("Certification and testimony requirements"). Subparagraph (B) requires the Secretary, with respect to each application processing cycle and prior to the initiation of that cycle, to:

- Under clause (i), on a date not later than September 1, certify to the authorizing committees either (I) that the Department will meet the October 1 deadline in subparagraph (A) for that cycle, or (II) that the Department will not meet that deadline; and
- Under clause (ii), in the case of a certification of anticipated non-compliance under clause (i)(II), on a date not later than September 30, testify before the authorizing committees regarding (I) the anticipated failure to meet the deadline and (II) the financial impact of that failure on students and families.

Section 1 designates the short title and is codified as a note to 20 U.S.C. 1001.

The Act contains no separate effective-date provision; its amendments therefore take effect upon enactment. It provides no authorization of appropriations and no appropriation. The bill is silent as to any enforcement mechanism or consequence attaching to a certification of non-compliance beyond the testimony requirement, and does not define "authorizing committees" within its text (relying on the term as used in the Higher Education Act). No provisions are repealed apart from the superseded deadline language, and no sunset is imposed.

Section 3 further amends section 483(d)(4) by designating the existing text as subparagraph (A) under the heading “In general” and adding a new subparagraph (B) titled “Certification and testimony requirements.” Under new subparagraph (B), the Secretary must, prior to the initiation of each application processing cycle, take the following actions: not later than September 1, certify to the authorizing committees either that the Department will meet the October 1 deadline or that it will not meet the deadline; and, in the case of a certification of anticipated failure, not later than September 30, testify before the authorizing committees on the anticipated failure and its financial impact on students and families. The term “authorizing committees” is not defined in the bill. The Act contains no authorization of appropriations, no sunset provision, and no delayed effective date; it took effect upon enactment on December 11, 2024.

This bill, the "Energy and Water Development and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2025," provides funding for energy and water programs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025. It is organized into five titles.

**Title I – Corps of Engineers (Civil):** Appropriates funds to the Army Corps of Engineers, including $159 million for investigations, $3.01 billion for construction, $370 million for Mississippi River and tributaries work, $5.714 billion for operation and maintenance, $218 million for the regulatory program, and $200 million for cleanup of early atomic-energy sites. Section 315 amends Natural Gas Act §3 (15 U.S.C. 717b), vesting FERC with exclusive authority over LNG export/import facility siting and deeming such trade consistent with the public interest, subject to a Presidential sanctions savings clause. expert.summary:
### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism

H.R. 8997, the Energy and Water Development and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2025, is a legislative measure that provides discretionary appropriations out of the U.S. Treasury for fiscal year (FY) 2025. Its primary purpose is to fund the civil works functions of the Department of the Army (Corps of Engineers), the Department of the Interior (including the Bureau of Reclamation and the Central Utah Project), the Department of Energy (DOE), and several independent regional and safety commissions. 

---

### Major Provisions by Title

#### Title I: Corps of Engineers—Civil
Title I appropriates funds to the Department of the Army, Corps of Engineers—Civil, for authorized civil functions, including:
*   **Investigations:** $159,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Construction:** $3,010,000,000, to remain available until expended, specifying that $34,900,000 be derived from the Harbor Maintenance Trust Fund and 35% of inland waterways project costs be derived from the Inland Waterways Trust Fund.
*   **Mississippi River and Tributaries:** $370,000,000, to remain available until expended, with $5,465,000 derived from the Harbor Maintenance Trust Fund.
*   **Operation and Maintenance:** $5,714,000,000, to remain available until expended, with $3,106,635,000 derived from the Harbor Maintenance Trust Fund. This includes $60,000,000 to carry out 33 U.S.C. 2238c(c), designated pursuant to Public Law 116-136.
*   **Regulatory Program:** $218,000,000, available until September 30, 2026.
*   **Formerly Utilized Sites Remedial Action Program (FUSRAP):** $200,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Flood Control and Coastal Emergencies:** $45,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Expenses:** $231,000,000, available until September 30, 2026.
*   **Office of the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works:** $5,000,000, available until September 30, 2026, authorized under 10 U.S.C. 7016(b)(3).
*   **Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program Account:** $5,000,000, available until September 30, 2026, for administrative expenses, notwithstanding section 5033 of the Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act of 2014.

**General Provisions (Title I):**
*   **Sec. 101:** Establishes statutory reprogramming thresholds and baseline reporting requirements. It prohibits reprogramming that creates, initiates, or eliminates programs, or increases funds for restricted activities without prior congressional approval.
*   **Sec. 104:** Authorizes the transfer of up to $8,733,000 from "Operation and Maintenance" to the Fish and Wildlife Service.
*   **Sec. 105:** Conditions the use of funds for open lake placement of dredged material in Lake Erie on state water quality certification under section 401 of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act (33 U.S.C. 1341).
*   **Sec. 108:** Mandates that the EPA and the Assistant Secretary of the Army for Civil Works provide guidance documents regarding the "Waters of the United States" conforming rule (88 Fed. Reg. 61964) within 15 days of enactment.
*   **Sec. 110:** Prohibits the enforcement of regulations restricting firearm possession at water resources development projects under 36 C.F.R. § 327.0, provided possession complies with state law and the individual is not otherwise legally prohibited.

#### Title II: Department of the Interior
Title II provides funding for water resources development and reclamation projects:
*   **Central Utah Project Completion Account:** $23,000,000, to remain available until expended, with $4,000,000 deposited into the Utah Reclamation Mitigation and Conservation Account.
*   **Bureau of Reclamation—Water and Related Resources:** $1,773,000,000, to remain available until expended, with designated transfers to the Upper Colorado River Basin Fund ($23,620,000) and the Lower Colorado River Basin Development Fund ($7,584,000). It directs $100,000 to the Aging Infrastructure Account under 43 U.S.C. 510b(d)(1) and $7,000,000 to the San Gabriel Basin Restoration Fund.
*   **Central Valley Project Restoration Fund:** Appropriates collected mitigation and restoration payments pursuant to Public Law 102-575.
*   **California Bay-Delta Restoration:** $33,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Policy and Administration:** $66,794,000, derived from the Reclamation Fund.

**General Provisions (Title II):**
*   **Sec. 201:** Restricts reprogramming of Bureau of Reclamation funds, establishing a 15% transfer limit for programs with budgets of $2,000,000 or more, and a $400,000 limit for programs under $2,000,000.
*   **Sec. 203 & 204:** Amends the Calfed Bay-Delta Authorization Act (P.L. 108-361) and the Reclamation States Emergency Drought Relief Act of 1991 (43 U.S.C. 2214(c), 2241) to extend authorizations through 2025, and increases the authorization of appropriations under 43 U.S.C. 2241 from $120,000,000 to $130,000,000.
*   **Sec. 205 & 206:** Prohibits consultation under section 7 of the Endangered Species Act (16 U.S.C. 1536) on the Central Valley Project and State Water Project operations until a comprehensive report is delivered to Congress. It mandates operations conform to the 2019 Preferred Alternative and FWS/NOAA Biological Opinions.
*   **Sec. 207:** Amends 43 U.S.C. 3202(a)(2) to strike eligibility exclusions for certain water storage projects under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
*   **Sec. 209:** Amends the Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation Act (P.L. 114-322) to extend the section 4007 storage project authority to 2026 and the section 4004 authority to December 16, 2034. It also increases the authorization of appropriations under the Reclamation Wastewater and Groundwater Study and Facilities Act (43 U.S.C. 390h) from $50,000,000 to $167,500,000, and the Water Desalination Act of 1996 from $30,000,000 to $100,500,000.

#### Title III: Department of Energy
Title III provides appropriations for DOE energy programs, atomic energy defense activities, and power marketing administrations:
*   **Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy:** $1,960,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response:** $200,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Electricity:** $250,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Nuclear Energy:** $1,793,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Fossil Energy and Carbon Management:** $875,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR):** $295,148,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Science:** $8,390,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Advanced Research Projects Agency—Energy (ARPA-E):** $450,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Title 17 Innovative Technology Loan Guarantee Program:** $55,000,000 for administrative expenses, offset by fees collected under 42 U.S.C. 16512(h) to yield a net appropriation of $0.
*   **National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA):** Appropriates $20,338,752,000 for Weapons Activities, $2,445,000,000 for Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation, $2,118,773,000 for Naval Reactors, and $564,475,000 for Federal Salaries and Expenses.
*   **Defense Environmental Cleanup:** $7,132,000,000, to remain available until expended.
*   **Power Marketing Administrations:** Authorizes expenditures from the Bonneville Power Administration Fund (prohibiting new direct loan obligations) and provides appropriations for the Southeastern ($0 net), Southwestern ($11,440,000 net), and Western Area ($99,872,000 net) Power Administrations, and the Falcon and Amistad Operating and Maintenance Fund ($228,000 net).
*   **Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC):** $532,000,000, fully offset by fees and annual charges to yield a net appropriation of $0.

**General Provisions (Title III):**
*   **Sec. 301:** Restricts reprogramming and requires a 3-day advance notification to Congress for discretionary grants, contracts, or laboratory funding allocations of $1,000,000 or more, and laboratory allocations of $25,000,000 or more.
*   **Sec. 307:** Prohibits the establishment of new regional petroleum product reserves unless explicitly requested in the President's budget and approved by Congress.
*   **Sec. 308:** Prohibits the drawdown and sale of SPR petroleum products to entities owned, controlled, or influenced by the Chinese Communist Party, or for export to the People's Republic of China.
*   **Sec. 309:** Prohibits DOE from awarding grants, contracts, or loans of $10,000,000 or more to an "entity of concern" under section 10114 of Public Law 117-167.
*   **Sec. 310:** Restricts the admittance of Russian or Chinese citizens to nuclear weapons production facilities (50 U.S.C. 2501) without a 30-day prior notification to Congress.
*   **Sec. 314:** Prohibits the expenditure of funds to support the DOE Justice40 initiative under Executive Order 14008.
*   **Sec. 315:** Amends section 3 of the Natural Gas Act (15 U.S.C. 717b) to grant the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission exclusive authority to approve or deny natural gas import/export facilities, deeming such actions consistent with the public interest, while preserving presidential sanction authorities.
*   **Sec. 317:** Directs the transfer of unobligated balances to "Nuclear Energy" for Generation 3+ small modular reactor deployment and Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program awards, including:
    *   $980,000,000 from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) Nuclear Energy balances.
    *   $1,500,000,000 from the IIJA Carbon Dioxide Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Program.
    *   $1,500,000,000 from section 50141 of Public Law 117-169 (amending the program's total funding to $25,000,000,000).
    *   $5,000,000,000 from section 50144 of Public Law 117-169 (amending the program's total funding to $5,000,000,000).

Public Law 118-94, the "Lake Tahoe Restoration Reauthorization Act" (S. 612), enacted October 1, 2024, extends the temporal availability of two authorities under the Lake Tahoe Restoration Act (Public Law 106-506). The Act's primary purpose is reauthorization; its operative mechanism consists of two conforming amendments to existing statutory text.

Section 2(a) amends Section 4(f) of the Lake Tahoe Restoration Act, which governs cooperative authorities. It strikes the existing durational limitation—"4 fiscal years following the date of enactment of the Water Resources Development Act of 2016"—and substitutes a period "beginning on the date of enactment of this subsection and ending on the date described in section 10(a)." Section 2(b) amends Section 10(a) of the Lake Tahoe Restoration Act, the authorization of appropriations provision. The Act does not itself appropriate funds; it operates solely on the authorization and availability framework of the underlying statute. It contains no new grant of substantive authority beyond the extension of the existing cooperative authorities under Section 4(f), and it specifies no additional exceptions, conditions precedent, or deadlines beyond the September 30, 2034 availability terminus that now anchors both amended provisions. No separate effective date is provided; the amendments take effect upon enactment on October 1, 2024.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
This bill, retitled the "Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act," establishes new federal requirements for online platforms used by minors and amends existing children's online privacy law. It has three titles.

**Title I – Keeping Kids Safe Online.** It defines a "covered platform" (online platforms, video games, messaging apps, and video streaming services likely used by minors, with numerous exceptions such as common carriers, email, schools, libraries, and nonprofits). A "minor" is anyone under 17; a "child" is under 13. Key provisions:
- **Duty of care:** Platforms must exercise reasonable care in designing features to prevent and mitigate specified harms to minors (e.g., certain mental health disorders, addiction-like use, bullying, sexual exploitation, and marketing of drugs, alcohol, tobacco, or gambling).
- **Safeguards:** Platforms must give known minors easy-to-use controls over communication, privacy, recommendation systems, and time spent, with the most protective settings on by default. Parental tools and reporting mechanisms (with response deadlines) are required.
- **Disclosure and transparency:** Platforms must provide notices and, for those averaging over 10 million U.S. monthly users, publish annual third-party-audited reports on risks to minors.
- It mandates studies (by the National Academy of Sciences, on age verification, and on market research), creates a Kids Online Safety Council, and authorizes enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general. The subtitle generally takes effect 18 months after enactment.

**Subtitle B – Filter Bubble Transparency** requires platforms using "opaque algorithms" (which rely on user-specific data not expressly provided) to notify users and offer an "input-transparent" alternative, effective one year after enactment.

**Title II – Children and Teens' Online Privacy** amends the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, extending protections to "teens" (ages 13–16), adding a "knowledge fairly implied" standard, expanding the definition of personal information, restricting individual-specific advertising, and adding deletion, correction, and data-security rights.

**Title III – Eliminating Useless Reports** amends title 31 to require agencies to identify outdated or duplicative recurring reports in budget justification materials and recommend changes.

The bill states it does not preempt stronger state protections and includes severability provisions.

This is a Senate amendment to the House amendment to S. 2073, substituting the entire text and retitling the bill the "Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act." The measure comprises three titles addressing minors' online safety, children's and teens' online privacy, and agency reporting requirements. Section 112 sets a general effective date of 18 months after enactment for Subtitle A of Title I unless otherwise provided.

**Title I, Subtitle A (Kids Online Safety).** Sections 101–113 impose obligations on "covered platforms"—online platforms, online video games, messaging applications, or video streaming services reasonably likely to be used by minors (defined as individuals under 17; "child" is under 13), with enumerated exceptions (common carriers, broadband, email, certain messaging/conferencing services, nonprofits, schools, libraries, news/sports apps, B2B software, and VPNs). Section 102 establishes a "duty of care" requiring reasonable care in designing features to prevent enumerated harms (specified mental-health disorders, compulsive use, violence/bullying, sexual exploitation, marketing of narcotics/tobacco/gambling/alcohol, and deceptive marketing), subject to a limitation preserving minors' independent searches. Section 103 mandates safeguards, default most-protective settings, parental tools (enabled by default for children), reporting mechanisms with tiered response deadlines (10/21 days by user count; imminent-threat immediacy), a dark-patterns prohibition, and advertising restrictions. Sections 104–105 require disclosures and, for platforms exceeding 10,000,000 monthly U.S. users, annual public transparency reports based on independent third-party audits. Sections 106–108 direct FTC contracts with the National Academy (using FTC Act §6(b) authority, 15 U.S.C. 46(b)), market-research guidance, and a Commerce/FCC/FTC age-verification study (report due 1 year). Section 110 treats violations as unfair or deceptive acts under FTC Act §18(a)(1)(B) and authorizes state attorney-general enforcement for §§103–105 (not §102). Section 111 establishes a Kids Online Safety Council, exempt from FACA. Section 113 preserves FERPA, COPPA, FTC Act §18(h), and §230, and disclaims any age-verification mandate.

**Subtitle B (§§120–121)** requires operators of online platforms using an "opaque algorithm" to provide notices and enable an "input-transparent algorithm" option, enforced as an FTC Act unfair/deceptive practice, effective 1 year after enactment. **Subtitle C (§§130–131)** provides conflict-only preemption (permitting greater state protections) and severability.

**Title II (§§201–204)** substantially amends the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (15 U.S.C. 6501 et seq.), extending coverage to "teens" (13–16), broadening "operator" and "personal information," adding a "knowledge fairly implied" standard, restricting individual-specific advertising, adding deletion/correction rights, and directing FTC guidance and studies (including a GAO fintech-privacy study).

**Title III (§301)** amends 31 U.S.C. 1125 (and conforming provisions of 31 U.S.C. 1105(a) and the James M. Inhofe NDAA for FY2023) to require agencies to identify outdated or duplicative recurring reports in budget justification materials, with recommendations to sunset, modify, or consolidate them.

The bill contains authorizations and directives but no explicit appropriation. The title is amended to "An Act to protect the safety and privacy of children on the internet."

The Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act primarily establishes federal duties for covered online services used by minors and expands the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (“COPPA”), while also revising federal reporting-sunset procedures.

Title I, subtitle A (“Kids Online Safety”), creates a freestanding regulatory regime for “covered platforms” used or reasonably likely to be used by minors under 17, excluding specified carriers, broadband, email, conferencing, nonprofit, educational, library, news/sports, business software, VPN, and related services (§101). Section 102 imposes a duty of reasonable care in creating and implementing design features to prevent and mitigate specified harms to minors, including enumerated mental health disorders, addiction-like use, violence/bullying/harassment, sexual exploitation and abuse, marketing of narcotics, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol, and financial harms, without requiring platforms to block deliberate searches or access to prevention resources. Section 103 requires minor safeguards, default protective settings, parental tools, reporting mechanisms with response deadlines, and prohibits facilitating advertisements for specified illegal or age-restricted products to known minors; it includes dark-pattern, gameplay, third-party control, and construction provisions. Sections 104 and 105 require notices, recommendation-system disclosures, ad labeling, parental/minor resources, and annual public risk/audit reports for large user-generated-content platforms. Sections 106–109 direct FTC/National Academy studies, market-research guidance, an age-verification study by Commerce/FCC/FTC, and FTC guidance. Section 110 makes violations enforceable by the FTC as violations of rules under FTC Act §18(a)(1)(B), 15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B), and authorizes State attorneys general to enforce §§103–105 subject to notice, intervention, and pendency limitations; State AGs may not base State-law liability on §102. Section 111 establishes a Kids Online Safety Council exempt from FACA. Subtitle A generally takes effect 18 months after enactment (§112) and includes nonpreemption of FERPA, COPPA, FTC Act §18(h), and Communications Act §230; it does not require age collection, age gating, or age verification (§113).

Title I, subtitle B requires, one year after enactment, online platforms using “opaque algorithms” to provide specified notices and allow users to switch to an “input-transparent algorithm,” without differential pricing; violations are FTC-enforceable (§§120–121). Subtitle C provides conflict preemption only, preserves more protective State laws, and includes severability (§§130–131).

Title II amends COPPA, 15 U.S.C. 6501–6505, to cover teens ages 13–16, online and mobile applications, expanded “personal information,” geolocation, connected devices, and “individual-specific advertising to children or teens” (§201). It prohibits covered operators with actual or fairly implied knowledge from collecting, using, disclosing, maintaining, retaining, or transferring children’s or teens’ personal information in specified ways, including individual-specific advertising, unnecessary collection, foreign storage/transfer without direct notice, and excessive retention; expands notice, verifiable-consent, access, deletion, correction, security, educational-agreement, safe-harbor publication, State-enforcement, and banking-enforcement provisions; and requires FTC guidance within 180 days and a common-consent feasibility report within one year. Sections 202 and 203 require FTC reports on application-platform oversight and COPPA enforcement and a GAO study on teen fintech privacy. Section 204 provides severability.

Title III amends 31 U.S.C. 1125 to require agencies to include in budget justification materials lists of recurring congressional plans or reports, identify outdated or duplicative reports, and recommend sunset, modification, consolidation, or reduced frequency, with citations, committee lists, and justifications; it preserves underlying submission duties. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 to conform electronic submission and OMB guidance requirements (§301).

expert.summary:
### Primary Purpose and Operative Mechanism

The "Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act" (S. 2073, Engrossed Amendment Senate) is a comprehensive regulatory framework designed to protect minors from online harms, enhance children's and teens' digital privacy, and establish algorithmic transparency. The bill operates by:
1. Imposing a statutory duty of care and mandatory safety defaults on "covered platforms" used by minors under age 17;
2. Requiring platforms utilizing "opaque algorithms" to provide opt-out mechanisms;
3. Substantially amending the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (COPPA) to extend privacy protections to teens aged 13 to 16; and
4. Amending federal agency reporting requirements under Title 31 of the United States Code.

---

### Title I: Keeping Kids Safe Online

#### Subtitle A — Kids Online Safety
*   **Operative Definitions (§ 101):** Defines a "minor" as an individual under age 17, and a "child" as under age 13. "Covered platform" encompasses online platforms, video games, messaging apps, and streaming services reasonably likely to be used by a minor. It expressly excludes common carriers, broadband providers, email services, non-profit entities, educational institutions, libraries, and certain business-to-business or cloud storage products. The knowledge standard ("knows") is defined as actual knowledge or knowledge fairly implied on the basis of objective circumstances.
*   **Duty of Care (§ 102):** Establishes a new statutory duty requiring covered platforms to exercise reasonable care in platform design to prevent and mitigate specified harms to minors, including clinical mental health disorders, addiction-like behaviors, physical violence, online bullying, sexual exploitation, and the promotion of illicit substances, gambling, or alcohol.
*   **Safeguards and Parental Tools (§ 103):** Mandates that platforms provide minors with default safety settings configured to the most protective level. Platforms must offer tools to restrict communication, limit compulsive design features (e.g., infinite scroll), opt out of personalized recommendation systems, and restrict geolocation tracking. Parents of children (under 13) must be provided with default-enabled tools to control privacy settings, view usage metrics, and restrict financial transactions. Platforms are prohibited from using "dark patterns" to subvert these controls.
*   **Reporting Mechanisms (§ 103(c)):** Platforms must establish a channel to receive and respond to reports of harm. Response deadlines are tiered: 10 days for platforms averaging over 10 million monthly active U.S. users, and 21 days for platforms below that threshold. Imminent safety threats require immediate responses.
*   **Disclosure and Transparency (§§ 104–105):** Platforms must provide clear disclosures regarding privacy policies and algorithmic risks prior to registration. For children under 13, platforms must obtain parental "verifiable consent" pursuant to COPPA. Platforms with over 10 million monthly active users must publish an annual public report based on an independent, third-party audit assessing risks and mitigation efficacy.
*   **Research, Guidance, and Administration (§§ 106–109, 111):** Directs the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to contract with the National Academy of Sciences for at least five scientific studies on social media harms, utilizing the FTC's investigative authority under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 46(b)). The Secretary of Commerce must establish a "Kids Online Safety Council" within 180 days of enactment to advise on emerging risks and standards; the Council is exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act (5 U.S.C. Chapter 10). The FTC, in coordination with other agencies, must issue compliance guidance within 18 months of enactment.
*   **Enforcement (§ 110):** Violations of Subtitle A are treated as unfair or deceptive acts or practices under Section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)). State Attorneys General are granted *parens patriae* authority to bring civil actions for injunctive relief, compliance, or damages in federal or state court, subject to providing prior written notice to the FTC. However, violations of the Section 102 duty of care are excluded from State Attorney General enforcement.
*   **Effective Date and Savings Provisions (§§ 112–113):** Subtitle A takes effect 18 months after enactment. It explicitly preserves the preemption profiles of COPPA, the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), and Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (47 U.S.C. 230). It clarifies that platforms are not required to implement age-gating or collect additional personal data to verify age.

#### Subtitle B — Filter Bubble Transparency
*   **Algorithmic Opt-Out (§§ 120–121):** Applies to online platforms using "opaque algorithms" (ranking systems utilizing user-specific data not expressly provided by the user). Effective one year after enactment, operators must provide clear notice of opaque algorithm use and enable users to easily switch to an "input-transparent algorithm" (which uses only user-supplied search terms, chronological ordering, or approximate geolocation). Platforms are prohibited from using differential pricing to penalize users who opt out of opaque algorithms. Violations are enforceable by the FTC as unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

#### Subtitle C — Relationship to State Laws; Severability
*   **Preemption and Severability (§§ 130–131):** Preempts state laws only to the extent they directly conflict with Title I, explicitly permitting states to enact measures that provide greater protection to minors. Includes a standard severability clause.

---

### Title II: Children and Teens' Online Privacy

*   **COPPA Amendments (§ 201):** Amends COPPA (15 U.S.C. 6501 et seq.) to establish a new protected class of "teens" (individuals aged 13 to 16). 
    *   *Knowledge Standard:* Elevates the COPPA threshold from "actual knowledge" to "actual knowledge or knowledge fairly implied on the basis of objective circumstances" (15 U.S.C. 6501(4)(B), 6502(a)(1)).
    *   *Targeted Advertising Ban:* Prohibits operators from collecting, using, disclosing, or maintaining the personal information of children or teens for "individual-specific advertising" (targeted behavioral advertising), subject to narrow exceptions for contextual advertising.
    *   *Data Minimization and Deletion:* Restricts data retention to the period reasonably necessary to fulfill a transaction. Operators must provide teens and parents of children the right to review, correct, and delete collected personal information. Service termination is prohibited if a user requests data deletion, provided the service can function without the deleted data.
    *   *Education Safe Harbor:* Permits operators to bypass direct parental consent requirements when acting under written agreements with educational agencies, provided data use is strictly limited to educational purposes.
*   **FTC Studies and Reports (§ 202):** Requires the FTC to submit an oversight report within three years of enactment regarding mobile application compliance, and an annual enforcement report detailing COPPA investigations, complaints, and legislative recommendations.
*   **GAO Study (§ 203):** Directs the Comptroller General of the United States to submit a report to Congress within one year of enactment analyzing the privacy risks posed to teens by financial technology products.

---

### Title III: Eliminating Useless Reports

*   **Statutory Sunsets and Agency Streamlining (§ 301):** Amends 31 U.S.C. 1125 to require federal agency heads to identify outdated or duplicative recurring congressional reports within their annual budget justification materials. Agency heads must provide recommendations to sunset, modify, or consolidate these reports. It also amends the James M. Title II amends the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) to extend privacy protections to teens (individuals aged 13 to 16). This bill, titled the Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act, primarily aims to establish new protections for minors on the internet by imposing requirements on certain online platforms and updating children’s privacy law, while also containing a separate title to reduce duplicative government reports.

Title I creates a “duty of care” for “covered platforms” (broadly defined as online platforms, video games, messaging apps, and video streaming services likely used by minors, with numerous exceptions for entities like internet service providers, email services, schools, and libraries). These platforms must exercise reasonable care in designing features to prevent and mitigate specific harms to minors, such as anxiety, depression, eating disorders, bullying, and sexual exploitation. The bill mandates that platforms provide minors with easy-to-use safeguards, set to the most protective levels by default, to limit unwanted communications, control personalized recommendation systems, restrict geolocation sharing, and manage time spent on the platform. Parental tools for managing privacy and account settings are also required, enabled by default for users under 13. Covered platforms must publish annual transparency reports based on independent third-party audits assessing risks of harm to minors. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and state attorneys general are given authority to enforce the act, which generally takes effect 18 months after enactment. The title also requires large online platforms that use opaque, user-data-driven algorithms to give users the option to switch to an “input-transparent algorithm” that primarily relies on information the user expressly provides. State laws are only preempted if they directly conflict with this title, and states may enact stronger protections.

Title II amends the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (COPPA) to extend its protections to teens aged 13 to 16, in addition to children under 13. It expands the definition of personal information to include items like photographs, voice recordings, and geolocation information. The bill prohibits operators from collecting, using, or disclosing a child or teen’s personal information for targeted advertising and requires that data not be retained longer than necessary. It establishes rights for parents and teens to access, correct, and delete personal information, and prohibits an operator from terminating service because a deletion request is made.

Title III requires federal agencies to include in their annual budget justifications a list of recurring reports to Congress, identify any that are outdated or duplicative, and provide a recommendation to sunset, modify, or consolidate them.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Improving Federal Building Security Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-157) requires Facility Security Committees to formally respond to security recommendations issued by the Federal Protective Service for non-military federal facilities. A Facility Security Committee consists of representatives of all federal tenants in a specific facility, the facility's security organization, and the owning or leasing federal tenant, and is responsible for addressing facility-specific security issues and approving security measures.

Under the law, within 90 days of receiving a security recommendation, the head of a Facility Security Committee (or a designee) must respond to the Secretary of Homeland Security indicating whether the committee intends to adopt or reject the recommendation and describing the financial implications, including a cost-benefit assessment. If the committee rejects a recommendation, it must provide a justification for accepting the resulting risk. The Secretary must develop a method to monitor these recommendations and responses and take reasonable action to ensure committees respond.

The law requires the Secretary to submit an annual report—within 270 days of enactment and annually thereafter—to specified Senate and House committees. Each report must summarize the recommendations issued, the percentages accepted, rejected, or not responded to in a timely manner, justifications for rejections, financial implications, steps taken to mitigate risks from rejections, and any trends. Reports are unclassified but may include a classified annex, and the Secretary must also provide an annual briefing.

Within 180 days of enactment, the Secretary must submit an unredacted report on all surveillance technology recommended by the Federal Protective Service and any intended uses.

No additional funds are authorized to carry out the Act. The law applies only to General Services Administration facilities protected by the Federal Protective Service and non-GSA facilities that pay the Service for protection. The Act sunsets five years after enactment, and the Comptroller General must report to Congress on its effectiveness within that same five-year period. The law was approved December 17, 2024.

The Improving Federal Building Security Act of 2024 (Pub. L. 118-157, enacted December 17, 2024, originating as S. 3613), codified as a note to 40 U.S.C. 1315, establishes a mandatory response-and-reporting regime governing Facility Security Committees' (FSCs) treatment of security recommendations issued by the Federal Protective Service (FPS). The Act operates as freestanding law rather than by direct amendment to the U.S. Code.

Section 2(a) supplies definitions, incorporating the definition of "agency" from 5 U.S.C. 551, defining "Facility Security Committee" as a committee comprising representatives of all Federal tenants in a specific non-military facility, the facility's security organization, and the owning or leasing Federal tenant, responsible for addressing facility-specific security issues and approving security measures; and designating the Secretary of Homeland Security as "Secretary."

Section 2(b) imposes a 90-day deadline, running from FPS issuance of a security recommendation, within which the head of the FSC (or designee) must respond to the Secretary indicating adoption or rejection, describing the financial implications (including a benefit-cost characterization), and—if rejecting—providing justification for accepting the residual risk. Subsection (b)(2) directs the Secretary to develop a monitoring method and take reasonable action to ensure FSC responsiveness.

Section 2(c) requires an annual report, due not later than 270 days after enactment and annually thereafter, to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and the House Committees on Homeland Security and on Transportation and Infrastructure. The report must, for the preceding fiscal year, summarize FPS recommendations; state acceptance and rejection percentages; state the percentage of FSCs failing to respond timely; summarize rejection justifications; summarize financial implications; analyze risk-mitigation steps taken upon rejection; and analyze trends. Reports are to be unclassified with an optional classified annex, accompanied by annual briefings to the same committees.

Section 2(d) requires the Secretary, not later than 180 days after enactment, to submit to the same committees an unredacted report on all surveillance technology recommended by FPS and any intended use.

Section 2(e) provides that no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out the Act (a negative authorization provision).

Section 2(f) sets a sunset: the Act ceases to be effective five years after enactment, and directs the Comptroller General to submit a report on the Act's effectiveness within the same five-year period.

Section 2(g) limits application to General Services Administration facilities under FPS protection and to non-GSA facilities that pay FPS protection fees.

anthropic__claude-opus-4.8.summary:
The Jamul Indian Village Land Transfer Act (Public Law 118-199) places approximately 172.10 acres of land in San Diego County, California, into trust by the United States for the benefit of the Jamul Indian Village of California, a federally recognized Indian Tribe.

The law identifies four specific parcels held in fee by the Tribe, described by recorded documents in the Office of the Recorder of San Diego County: Parcel 1 (approximately 161.23 acres), Parcel 2 (approximately 6 acres), Parcel 3 (approximately 4.03 acres), and Parcel 4 (approximately 0.84 acres). These parcels are placed directly into trust by operation of the Act.

In addition, the Act directs the Secretary of the Interior to accept title to and place into trust an additional parcel of approximately 1.1 acres—depicted as "Proposed 1.1 acres" on a California Department of Fish and Wildlife map titled "Amended Acres Proposal," dated May 2023—but only if that land is conveyed or transferred to the United States by or on behalf of the Tribe.

All land taken into trust under the Act becomes part of the Jamul Indian Village's reservation and is administered according to the laws and regulations generally applicable to property held in trust by the United States for an Indian Tribe.

The Act prohibits the use of all the described land for any class II or class III gaming as those terms are defined under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.

The law was approved December 23, 2024. It originated as S. 3857, was passed by the Senate on December 12, 2024, and by the House on December 17 and 18, 2024.

expert.summary:
Public Law 118-199, the "Jamul Indian Village Land Transfer Act" (S. 3857), effects a statutory taking of land into trust by the United States for the benefit of the Jamul Indian Village of California, in San Diego County, California. Rather than proceeding through the discretionary administrative fee-to-trust process under 25 U.S.C. 5108 and 25 C.F.R. Part 151, the Act directly mandates trust status by operation of law.

Section 2(a) provides that approximately 172.10 acres described in subsection (b) "is held in trust" by the United States for the Tribe. Subsection (b) enumerates four parcels by recorded document number in the Official Records of the San Diego County Recorder: Parcel 1 (approximately 161.23 acres, Doc. No. 2022-0010260, recorded January 7, 2022); Parcel 2 (approximately 6 acres, Doc. No. 2021-0540770, recorded July 29, 2021); Parcel 3 (approximately 4.03 acres, Doc. No. 1998-0020339, recorded January 15, 1998); and Parcel 4 (approximately 0.84 acres, Doc. No. 2017-0410384, recorded September 7, 2017). Parcels 1 and 2 are identified as held in fee by the Tribe.

Section 2(c) directs the Secretary of the Interior to accept title to and place into trust an additional approximately 1.1-acre parcel depicted on the California Department of Fish and Wildlife map "Amended Acres Proposal" (dated May 2023). This additional trust acquisition is subject to a condition precedent: it applies only "if that land is conveyed or otherwise transferred to the United States by, or on behalf of," the Tribe.

Section 2(d) provides that land taken into trust under both subsections (a) and (c) shall be part of the Tribe's reservation and administered under the laws and regulations generally applicable to trust property held for an Indian Tribe.

Section 2(e) imposes a gaming prohibition: land described in subsections (b) and (c) shall not be used for any class II or class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (25 U.S.C. 2701 et seq.), applying the definitions in section 4 of that Act (25 U.S.C. 2703). The Act does not reference the class III gaming compact framework or the section 20 exceptions.

The Act contains no appropriation, authorization of appropriations, sunset provision, or specified effective date; the trust status conferred by subsection (a) operates upon enactment. Approved December 23, 2024.

eli5.summary:
This resolution is Congress saying it does not agree with a recent government rule. The rule was made by the Federal Highway Administration, the agency that helps build and fix highways. The rule would have created a waiver, or an exception, to "Buy America" rules for electric vehicle chargers. Buy America rules say that when the government pays for certain projects, the materials and products must be made in the United States. The waiver would have allowed chargers to be bought even if they were not made in America.

The rule was published on February 21, 2023. This resolution says Congress disapproves, or rejects, that rule. If the resolution passes both the Senate and the House of Representatives and is signed by the President, the rule will have no force or effect. That means the waiver would be canceled, and the Buy America requirements would stay in place for electric vehicle chargers. The Senate passed this resolution on November 8, 2023.

expert.summary:
S.J. Res. 38, as passed by the Senate on November 8, 2023, is a joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code (the Congressional Review Act). The resolution exercises the legislative veto mechanism of the Congressional Review Act to nullify a specific final rule issued by the Federal Highway Administration. The operative provision states: “Congress disapproves the rule submitted by the Federal Highway Administration relating to ‘Waiver of Buy America Requirements for Electric Vehicle Chargers’ (88 Fed. Reg. 10619 (February 21, 2023)), and such rule shall have no force or effect.” The resolution does not amend any section of the United States Code; it acts directly on the agency rule.

Upon enactment, the disapproval would trigger the statutory bar in 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(2), prohibiting the Federal Highway Administration from reissuing the disapproved rule in substantially the same form, or issuing a new rule that is substantially the same, unless specifically authorized by a subsequent law. The resolution contains no exceptions, conditions precedent, delayed effective dates, or sunset provisions. It authorizes no appropriations and does not itself provide any funding. The resolution’s effect is immediate upon enactment, subject to the Congressional Review Act’s expedited procedures and the presentment requirements applicable to joint resolutions.

crs_reference.summary:
This joint resolution nullifies the final rule issued by the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) titled Waiver of Buy America Requirements for Electric Vehicle Chargers and published on February 21, 2023. The rule temporarily waives the Buy America requirements for steel, iron, manufactured products, and construction materials in electric vehicle (EV) chargers. 
FHWA defines an EV charger to mean the EV charger unit itself and the equipment contained inside it. EV charger housing components that are predominantly steel and iron are excluded from the waiver and must meet current FHWA Buy America requirements. 
The FHWA final rule waives Buy America requirements for all EV chargers and components that are manufactured from the effective date of this waiver until June 30, 2024. Further, the final assembly must occur in the United States, and the installation must begin by October 1, 2024. 
Beginning with EV chargers manufactured on July 1, 2024, the FHWA phases out waiver coverage for those previously covered EV chargers where the cost of U.S. manufactured components does not exceed 55% of the total components cost. (Under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, more than 55% of the components of manufactured goods must be obtained from U.S. manufacturers and sources.) 
This waiver remains in place until terminated by the FHWA.

prompts.judge:
You are a meticulous evaluator applying the Congressional Research Service's quality standards to a summary of a U.S. bill. CRS holds summaries to a high bar: they must be accurate, complete, neutral, and faithful to the legislative text — while also providing useful real-world context.

You are given (1) the full BILL TEXT, which is the ground truth for what the bill DOES, and (2) a SUMMARY to evaluate.

IMPORTANT — context is allowed. A good summary may include accurate real-world context that is not literally in the bill text: the common name of a program, the agency that administers it, the statute being amended, what an existing program does, etc. This is a strength, not a hallucination. Use your own knowledge and the web search tool available to you to VERIFY such contextual claims. Fail an accuracy/hallucination criterion only when a claim CONTRADICTS the bill text or is factually FALSE or fabricated — never merely because a (true) fact is absent from the bill text. Likewise, do not penalize a faithful high-level summary for omitting granular figures or minor sub-provisions, as long as it captures the bill's essential effect.

For EACH criterion below, decide:
- "applicable": true/false. For criteria marked (conditional), first decide whether the criterion is relevant to THIS bill (e.g. "Effective dates" is not applicable if the bill specifies no dates). Criteria marked (always) are always applicable.
- "pass": true/false. If applicable is false, set pass to true. Otherwise pass is true only if the summary satisfies the criterion as described.
- "why": one short sentence justifying the verdict, citing the specific issue when failing.

Be discerning: a claim that contradicts the bill or is factually wrong fails; a wrong number fails "correct_figures"; but accurate added context and reasonable high-level summarization should pass.

CRITERIA:
{criteria_block}

BILL TEXT (ground truth):
---
{bill_text}
---

SUMMARY TO EVALUATE:
---
{summary}
---

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no markdown fences, of this exact shape:
{{"verdicts": {{"<criterion_id>": {{"applicable": true, "pass": true, "why": "..."}}, ...}}}}
Include every criterion id. Output nothing else.
